form-field.name: Form field
form-field.description: The label, the description and the error around one control, and the wiring that makes them true for a screen reader: the label is a real label for the control, the description and the error are what it is described by, and an error marks it invalid and is announced once. A TextField, Select, SearchField, Checkbox, Switch or RadioGroup inside it reads what it needs; a field that is not inside one keeps drawing its own label and helper.

label.description: The field's name: a real label for the control inside. A control with a name of its own (a Checkbox, a Switch) keeps it; the label then names the field around it.

description.description: One clause under the label that says what to enter or why. Read after the control's name.
description.sample: We send invoices and renewal notices here.

error.description: What is wrong and how to fix it. While it is not empty the control is marked invalid and the message is announced once, politely. Say it in a sentence: "Enter an address like name@company.com".

required.description: Marks the control required (aria-required; the phone reads it after the name) and draws a "Required" pill beside the label. The pill is hidden from screen readers: the state is the attribute.

hideLabel.description: Keep the label for screen readers but do not draw it, when a heading above already asks the question.

children.description: The one control: a TextField, Select, SearchField, Checkbox, Switch or RadioGroup. It takes its id, its description and error, and aria-invalid and aria-required from the field.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: The label is a real <label for> pointing at the control (the phone: the control's accessibility label, when it has none).

The description and the error are the control's aria-describedby (the phone: its hint), so they are read after its name when it takes focus. The field itself is not a landmark or a group: the control inside is the one thing a screen reader moves to.
An error is announced once, politely, when it arrives, and the control is marked aria-invalid while it shows. Nothing is announced on each keystroke.
Required is aria-required on the control; the visible pill is hidden from screen readers so it is not read twice. A Switch has no required state, so the field does not set one.

props.label: Sound
props.description: Plays when a message in a channel you follow arrives.

examples.name: Label hidden
examples.description: The label is still the control's name; a heading above asks the question.

edgeCases.title: A control with its own label
edgeCases.handling: A Checkbox or a Switch always has a name of its own, and keeps it: the field's label then names the field around it and the control adds nothing to it. A TextField that draws its own label inside a field gets two names; give it none and let the field name it.

edgeCases.title: A long label or a long error
edgeCases.handling: Both wrap to as many lines as they need. An error is never truncated: the cut-off half is usually the instruction. The Required pill keeps its width and the label gives way.

edgeCases.title: An error that arrives while the control has focus
edgeCases.handling: It is announced once through the page's polite region (the phone: announceForAccessibility) and the control is marked invalid. Focus does not move: a validation message must not take the cursor away from the field being fixed. A form that refuses a submit moves focus to the first invalid control itself.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left
edgeCases.handling: The label sits at the start edge and the Required pill at the end, and the error's icon sits before its text. A text field inside lays an address, a number or a password out left to right.

web.base: A <div> with a <label for> over the control, a description and an error; a context carries the control's id, the ids of the description and the error (for aria-describedby), `invalid` and `required` to whichever control is inside; the error is announced through the page's polite live region
notes: A control inside reads the field with `useFormField()`; a product's own control can too, to take the same wiring.
A control that is not a native field (a Select's trigger, a RadioGroup) is named with aria-labelledby pointing at the label; a TextField and a SearchField are named by the label's `for`.

A Checkbox and a Switch keep their own label; the field adds its description and error to what they are described by. aria-invalid is set on every control that supports it, and aria-required on every control that supports it (not a Switch).

keyboard.action: Moves into the control; the label, the description and the error are not tab stops

desktop.base: The same field as web
notes: The label is a real label, so a click on it focuses a text field and presses a checkbox, as in the browser.

mobile.base: A View with a Text label, a description and an error; a context carries the field's label and one hint (the description, the error and "Required") to the control inside, which reads it as its accessibility label (when it has none) and hint; the error is announced with announceForAccessibility because iOS has no live regions
notes: The phone has no aria-invalid or aria-required: the hint is how a screen reader hears them, after the name.
The label and the messages scale with the person's text size, up to 2×.

gestures.action: On the control, as without a field; the label is not a target

gauge-chart.name: GaugeChart
gauge-chart.description: One value against a target on a half ring: the fill is a series colour while it is fine, the caution colour and then the loss colour as it crosses the thresholds (Meter's, so a gauge and a meter agree), with a tick at the target, the value and what it is of in the middle, and 0, the target and the most under it. It is for one number worth a ring; a number beside others is a Meter, and its history is a LineChart.

headingLevel.description: The heading level of the card's title, 1 to 6, so the chart keeps the page's heading order: a card under an h2 is an h3, one under an h1 is an h2. The phone has one kind of header and reads it for nothing. The card is not a landmark: the figure inside is named by the summary.

value.description: What there is, in the same unit as `max`. A value that is not a number draws the empty state. A value past `max` fills the ring and stops there, and the text says the real number.

max.description: What a full ring is: 1 when the value is already a share (the default, so 0.583 is 58.3%), or a capacity or a goal in the value's own unit.

target.description: Where the tick sits, in the value's unit: the goal the value is measured against. Left out, there is no tick and no "Target" under the ring. A target past `max` is drawn at its end.

title.description: The card's title. It names the figure on the page, and is the first words of what a screen reader hears.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: what it covers. Empty draws none.

headline.description: A number to lead with, under the title: { value, format, delta, deltaFormat, inverse, period }. It is a MetricValue (in the chart's format unless it names one), a Delta badge and what the change is against ("resolved in October"). Left out, the card has none.

label.description: What the value is of, under it in the hole. Empty draws only the number.

kind.description: `score` (a goal, a health rating) is fine while high and turns as it falls; `usage` (seats, storage, a quota) is fine while low and turns as it fills. Meter's two kinds, with Meter's thresholds. The fine colour is the third series colour for a score and the first for usage.

thresholds.description: The shares of `max` where the fill turns to the caution colour and then the loss colour: { warning: 0.5, danger: 0.4 }. Default Meter's for the kind: usage 0.75 and 0.9, a score 0.6 and 0.4.

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. The value, the target, the two ends, the summary and "View as table" all print through it, so they agree. A percent format prints each as its share of `max`, as Meter does: 58 of 100 is 58%.

size.description: The half ring's width, in px (points on the phone); its height is half. Default 280 on the web and desktop, 220 on the phone: `chart.gaugeW`.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when the value is not a number.

emptyLine.description: One sentence under it: what to do about it.
emptyLine.default: It shows once there is a number to measure.

loading.description: Grey bars of uneven heights in place of the plot, from the kit's Skeleton, and no "View as table". The header stays, so the card does not jump when the data arrives. Screen readers hear "Loading chart" once.

a11y.label: The summary: "Resolved by Fabric: 58.3% of resolved tickets, target 60%."
notes: The figure (the ring on the phone) is named by the sentence core's `summarizeGauge` writes: the value in the chart's format, what it is of, and the target. It is heard, not printed: the value and the target are already in the hole and under the ring.

The colour is never the only signal: the number is in the hole, the target is a tick and a caption ("Target 60%"), and a value past `max` says so in the summary ("over the 100% it is measured against").
"View as table" is the other way in: the measure, its value and its target, with real headers.
The numbers in the hole and under the ring are for the eye: the summary says them once for a screen reader.

examples.name: Resolved by Fabric
examples.description: 58.3% against Q4's 60%: above the caution line, so the fill is a series colour, and the tick is the target.

examples.name: With a headline
examples.description: The card leads with a number, its change and what it is against; the ring says how much of the whole it is.

headline.period: tickets resolved by Fabric, vs September

examples.name: A caution
examples.description: 46% is between the 40% and 50% lines: the caution colour.

examples.name: A loss
examples.description: 31% is under the 40% line: the loss colour.

props.label: of resolved tickets
props.title: Resolved by Fabric
props.subtitle: Fabric was offline for a day

examples.name: Seats in use, a usage gauge
examples.description: `kind: "usage"` fills toward the limit: 42 of 50 seats is past the 75% line, so it is the caution colour. The format prints seats, not a share.

props.title: Seats in use
props.subtitle: Northwind Logistics
props.label: of the seats on the plan

edgeCases.title: A value that is not a number
edgeCases.handling: A value that is not a number (a request that failed, a rate with no tickets to divide) draws the kit's EmptyState in the plot's place and says why (the title and line are props); the card keeps its header and has no "View as table". The figure's label says there is no value.

edgeCases.title: A value over max
edgeCases.handling: A value past `max` fills the ring and stops there: the ring cannot be fuller. The number in the hole says the real value (112%), and the summary says it is over what it is measured against. A score over its max is fine; a usage gauge over it is in the loss colour.

edgeCases.title: Zero
edgeCases.handling: Nothing fills the ring: it is the empty track, with the number 0% in the hole. A score at zero is in the loss colour, but with no fill to show it the number is the signal.

edgeCases.title: A target past the end
edgeCases.handling: A target past `max` is drawn at the ring's end, and the caption still says the number. A target of nothing is at the start. No target at all draws no tick and no caption, only 0 and the most.

edgeCases.title: Loading
edgeCases.handling: Grey bars of uneven heights fill the plot and the card keeps its header. There is no "View as table" and no summary yet. A screen reader hears "Loading chart" once.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section>: the title, an optional headline, "View as table" (Button); a ChartFrame holding recharts' PieChart with one Pie from 180 degrees to 0 (round ends, a hair of gap between fill and track) and an SVG <line> for the target, MetricValue in the hole and three captions under it
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is reached only from there. The ring is handed an explicit width and height, never a responsive container.

The fill is `tokens.data.warning` or `data.negative` once the share crosses a threshold, and a series colour otherwise, so a gauge reads the same as the Meter that shows the same number; no colour of the brand is read.
The fill draws in from the left over 600ms on the kit's ease-out and tweens to a new value; the number in the hole eases with it (MetricValue). Reduced motion turns both off.
The tick is drawn across the band and a little past it on both sides (`chart.tickOver`), so it reads as a mark on the ring and not a gap in it.

desktop.base: The same Card, recharts' Pie and tick as web, at desktop density

mobile.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a View: the same header and Button, a ChartFrame holding react-native-gifted-charts' PieChart `donut` with `semiCircle` (the hole a disc in the card's colour), a react-native-svg <Line> for the target, MetricValue in the hole and three captions under it
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: gifted-charts and react-native-svg are reached only from there.
gifted-charts draws a half ring as a whole pie, in a view half as tall that crops it; the kit lays that view `chart.tickOver` down in a taller one so the tick has room above the ring.
gifted-charts' slices have square ends, so the fill and the track meet in a straight cut, not the web's round ends. That is the one difference in the drawing.
The ring pops in over 220ms unless the person reduces motion.

In the catalogue, where the phone kit is drawn through react-native-web, a half ring would be shrunk into its half-height view instead of cropped by it. The catalogue's react-native-svg stand-in sets `flex-shrink: 0` on every svg it draws, so the svg keeps its size and the view crops it, as it does on a device; nothing is done to the kit's own code.

goal-rings.name: GoalRings
goal-rings.description: Up to three goals as nested rings, each filled as far as it has got, with the overall share in the middle and every goal listed beside the rings (below them on the phone) with what is done of its target and what is left, or "Goal met". Pointing at a goal (or its ring) lights it and pressing it picks it: the others step back and the middle eases to that goal's own share. "View as table" shows each goal's done and target in Table.

headingLevel.description: The heading level of the card's title, 1 to 6, so the chart keeps the page's heading order: a card under an h2 is an h3, one under an h1 is an h2. The phone has one kind of header and reads it for nothing. The card is not a landmark: the figure inside is named by the summary.

data.description: Rows, one per goal, in order: [{ goal: "Tickets resolved by Fabric", done: 455, target: 600 }, …]. The first three are drawn, outermost first, each in the next colour of the palette. The same rows can feed a table.

name.description: The field of each row that names its goal.

value.description: The field of each row that is what is done. A value that is not a number counts as 0.

goal.description: The field of each row that is its target. A target of 0, or one that is not a number, is no goal: the ring is its empty track and the list says "No goal set".

title.description: The card's title. It names the figure on the page, and is the first words of what a screen reader hears.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: what it covers. Empty draws none.

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. What is done, the target, what is left, the summary and "View as table" print through it. The shares are always whole percents.

valueLabel.description: The done column's name in "View as table".

goalLabel.description: The target column's name in "View as table".

centerLabel.description: What the middle says above the overall share. It says "This goal" while a goal is lit.

selected.description: The goal that is picked, by its name: the middle shows its share and the other rings and goals step back until it is picked again. Pointing at a goal or tabbing to it lights it too, for as long as the pointer or the keyboard is there. Left out, the chart keeps its own, starting with none. Controlled when the app passes it with `onSelectedChange`.

onSelectedChange.description: A ring or a goal was pressed. Called with the goal's name, or with null when it was already the one picked.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when there are no rows. Say why: nothing yet and nothing matching a filter are different sentences.

emptyLine.description: One sentence under it: what to do about it.
emptyLine.default: Add a goal to see how far along it is.

loading.description: Grey bars in place of the rings and the list, from the kit's Skeleton, and no "View as table". The header stays, so the card does not jump when the data arrives. Screen readers hear it once.

a11y.role: figure (web), one image and a list (phone)
a11y.label: The summary: "Fabric's Q4 goals: Tickets resolved by Fabric 455 of 600 (76%); Approvals cleared within a day 128 of 150 (85%); Docs questions answered 1,940 of 2,500 (78%); 80% done overall."
notes: The figure (the rings on the phone) is named by the sentence core's `summarizeGoals` writes from the rows: each goal, what is done of its target and its share, and the overall share. It is heard, not printed: the list beside the rings prints each goal's name, what is done, the target and what is left, so colour is never the only way in.

Each goal in the list is a button that says its own sentence ("Approvals cleared within a day, 128 of 150, 22 to go"), pressed while it is the one picked, and is a stop in the Tab order, so a keyboard can light and pick a goal as a pointer does. On the phone it is selected while it is the one picked.
"Goal met" is words, not only a full ring; the ring's colour is the goal's key, and the list names every goal beside its swatch.
The middle is drawn for the eye and hidden from a screen reader (it repeats the summary).
"View as table" is the other way in: each goal with what is done and its target, with real headers.

examples.name: Fabric's Q4 goals
examples.description: Three goals as nested rings, the overall share in the middle and each goal listed with what is left.

examples.name: A goal picked
examples.description: `selected` is the second goal: the middle shows its own share under "This goal", and the other rings and goals step back.

examples.name: Two goals
examples.description: Two rings: the first is outermost, each still in its own colour.

edgeCases.title: No goals
edgeCases.handling: An empty `data` draws the kit's EmptyState in the plot's place and says why (the title and line are props); the card keeps its header, and has no "View as table", since there is nothing to show. The figure's label says there are no goals.

edgeCases.title: One goal
edgeCases.handling: One goal is one ring, the outermost, in the first colour of the palette; the middle's share is that goal's own.

edgeCases.title: A goal over 100%
edgeCases.handling: A ring never runs past full, so a goal that has been passed is a full ring and the list says "Goal met" with the numbers as they are (2,900 / 2,500). It counts as whole in the overall share, so it cannot make up for a goal that is behind. The summary says the real percent (116%).

edgeCases.title: A goal with no target
edgeCases.handling: A target of 0, or one that is not a number, is no goal to be a share of: the ring is its empty track, the list says "No goal set" with no numbers, the summary says it has no goal, and it counts as 0 in the overall share.

edgeCases.title: More than three goals
edgeCases.handling: A fourth band would be too thin to read, so the first three rows are the rings and the rest are left out of the rings, the list and the summary. "View as table" has every row.

edgeCases.title: A long name
edgeCases.handling: A goal's name wraps on the web and the desktop and is cut with an ellipsis on the phone, where the numbers stay on its line; the summary and the table have the whole name.

edgeCases.title: Loading
edgeCases.handling: Grey bars of uneven heights fill the plot and the card keeps its header. There is no list, no table button and no summary yet. A screen reader hears "Loading chart" once.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section>: the title and "View as table" (Button); a ChartFrame holding one recharts PieChart with a track Pie and a value Pie per ring (round ends, 90 degrees round to -270), MetricValue in the middle, and a list of goals (<button> rows, aria-pressed) beside it
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is reached only from there. The rings are handed an explicit size, never a responsive container.

Each band is `chart.ringW` thick with `chart.ringGap` between it and the next ring in; the outermost is the first goal. A ring is its value Pie over a whole track Pie, so the round end of a value sits on the track.

The overall share is the mean of the rings' fill: a goal that is passed counts as whole and cannot make up for one that is not. Pointing at a ring or at its goal (or tabbing to it) lights it: the other rings and goals fade to 38% over 150ms on the kit's ease-out, and the middle's number eases to that goal's own share (MetricValue) under "This goal".
The rings draw in once over 600ms on the kit's ease-out. Reduced motion turns it off.
The list sits beside the rings and drops under them when the card is narrower than the rings, the gap and `chart.listMinW`.

keyboard.action: Moves through the goals in the list, then to "View as table". A goal that has focus is lit, and so is its ring
On a goal: picks it, or puts it back when it was picked

desktop.base: The same Card, recharts' PieChart and list as web, at desktop density
notes: The same chart as the web's. The pointer's hover lights a ring or a goal, and a click picks it.

keyboard.action: Moves through the goals in the list, then to "View as table". A goal that has focus is lit, and so is its ring
On a goal: picks it, or puts it back when it was picked

mobile.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a View: the same header and Button, a ChartFrame holding one react-native-gifted-charts PieChart `donut` per ring, stacked in views as wide as each ring's outer edge (each starts at 12 o'clock), MetricValue in the middle, and the goals below as Pressable rows
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: gifted-charts and react-native-svg are reached only from there. The rings are a little larger than the web's (`chart.ringSize` is 200pt, `chart.ringW` 15pt).
gifted-charts' slices have square ends, so the rings have none of the web's round ones. The list is below the rings, full width, each goal at least 44pt tall.

A phone has no hover, so a tap on a ring or on a goal picks it (the others step back to 38% and the middle shows its share, and `onSelectedChange` is called) and a tap on it again puts it back. gifted-charts' own press reads page coordinates on the web, which are wrong wherever the chart is not at the page's corner, so the kit finds the ring from where the touch landed in the square (`ringAt`).
The rings pop in over 220ms unless the person reduces motion: gifted-charts' pie draws no sweep of its own.

gestures.action: Picks its goal: the middle shows its share and the other rings step back. Tap it again to put it back

gestures.gesture: Tap a goal in the list
gestures.action: The same as tapping its ring

flows.title: Look at the approvals goal

hover-card.name: Hover card
hover-card.description: Who someone is, without leaving the conversation: rest the pointer on a name or an avatar (360 ms in the kit; the app's own is 380) or tab to it and a 260px card shows their face, name, title, presence, local time and status, with Message and View profile. The card sits flush with its trigger, so the pointer can move into it without closing it.

name.description: From the one profile source. Never an id: "Unknown user" when nothing resolves it.

src.description: Photo URL. Initials until it decodes.

title.description: Job title and team from the HR directory. Empty draws no line.

presence.description: Spelled out as a word beside a 9px dot. Away and offline use the same hollow dot on purpose; the word tells them apart. unknown is while this device is offline: no dot and no word, rather than a stale one.

localTime.description: Their wall-clock time, in your time format. Empty when the profile has no timezone, and the line then reads presence alone.

statusText.description: Their own status. Empty draws no line at all, not a placeholder.

statusUntil.description: The expiry, appended after a middle dot. Comes from expiryLabel so it reads the same as the sidebar's.

agent.description: An AI agent such as Fabric: the sparkle badge, the word Agent on a coral dot, no local time and no profile button.

guest.description: Someone from outside the organisation. A square Guest tag after the name.

self.description: Your own card. Message becomes Message yourself (AntFabric's copy says Open your space).

deleted.description: A deleted account. The card still opens (their old messages are on screen) but offers no Message, because that DM would be dropped by the next sidebar refresh.

placement.description: Set by the caller, not measured: up for a trigger near the bottom of a list.

showTrigger.description: With no children: draws the name the card was opened from, above or below the card.

children.description: What the card hangs from (a name, an avatar, an @mention). The card floats beside it, opens on its hover after a short rest and on keyboard focus, closes on Esc, blur and leave, and the trigger is aria-describedby it while it is open.

open.description: The card is showing. Hover and keyboard focus change it; set it to draw the card open (the catalogue does).

a11y.label: {name}
notes: The trigger (your `children`, or the built-in name button) is described by the card while it is open (aria-describedby), not marked aria-haspopup: this is a description of a person, not a menu.

The card is a labelled group, not role=tooltip: it holds two buttons, and ARIA does not allow controls inside a tooltip. It opens after a 360 ms rest on hover and at once on keyboard focus, closes on Esc, blur and leave, and is hoverable (it sits flush with the trigger inside the same host). Avatars beside the name are hidden from assistive tech.
Everything in the card is reachable without it: the name opens the profile and the profile has Message. The card is a shortcut, never the only way.
Presence is a word, never the dot alone.

props.name: Fabric
props.title: AI agent · answers from your workspace

edgeCases.title: Sweeping the pointer down a list of authors
edgeCases.handling: Nothing opens until the pointer rests for 380 ms, so dragging across ten names opens none. Leaving the trigger waits 180 ms before closing, long enough to cross the 6px gap; entering the panel cancels the close. Avatar and name triggers carry data-tip="" so the 320 ms tooltip never arrives first and covers the card.

edgeCases.title: A row near the bottom of the list
edgeCases.handling: The desktop caller passes placement="up", because flipping automatically needs the panel's height before it renders, and guessing is how a card ends up half off-screen the other way. The web's Positioner flips on its own and treats the prop as the preferred side.

edgeCases.title: Long name, title and status
edgeCases.handling: The name and the title each stay on one line and end in an ellipsis; the name's line height is the body leading, not 1, so descenders are not clipped. The status wraps to two lines, then truncates. The card never grows wider than 260px.

edgeCases.title: Your own card
edgeCases.handling: Hovering your own name on a message you wrote opens your card. Message reads Open your space, which opens your notes-to-self conversation; View profile goes to your own profile.

edgeCases.title: A deleted account
edgeCases.handling: Their old messages are still on screen, so the card still opens, reading Deleted user in the neutral ink colour with no presence, status or time. There is no Message button: the sidebar drops a DM with a deleted account on its next refresh, so the button would create a conversation and lose it a moment later.

edgeCases.title: Keyboard only and screen readers
edgeCases.handling: Focus on the trigger opens the card after the same delay, so a keyboard user gets the same card. Tab moves into Message and View profile; Esc closes it at once and stops there, so Esc does not also close the thread panel or dialog behind. A screen reader hears the name and title as the trigger's description, not a tooltip.

edgeCases.title: Touch screen on a laptop
edgeCases.handling: With pointer: coarse (a Surface, a touch Chromebook) there is no hover to rest on. A tap on the name or avatar opens the card at once with no delay; a tap outside closes it; tapping the trigger again follows its own action. The 26px buttons are too small for a finger, so while the pointer is coarse they grow to the md control height (34px desktop, 36px web).

edgeCases.title: Offline, or presence and timezone not known
edgeCases.handling: While this device is offline, other people's presence is unknown, so the line shows the local time alone (worked out on this device from the cached timezone) rather than a stale Active. The desktop draws the name, title and status from its SQLite cache; an expired status is dropped when it is read, not shown with a past until. With no timezone on the profile, the time is left out and the presence word stands alone.

web.base: A labelled role="group" card that the trigger points at with aria-describedby: Avatar and two secondary Buttons, inline styles over `t`; pops in with enter("pop"); Esc calls onClose and stops there. The open and close delays are the app's
notes: Same card, same timings and the same two buttons as desktop.

Opens on hover only where (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine). Under pointer: coarse (a touch laptop, a tablet with a trackpad detached) a tap on the name or avatar opens it at once, a tap outside closes it, and a second tap on the trigger follows its own action (opens the profile).
The Positioner flips and shifts to stay 8px inside the viewport, so the web does not need the caller's placement; the prop is kept for parity and as the preferred side.
View profile is a real link (<a href="/people/…">), so ⌘-click and middle-click open the profile in a new tab.

keyboard.action: Opens after the same 380 ms; focus stays on the trigger
Moves into Message, then View profile; leaving the card closes it after 180 ms
Closes at once and stops there, so the dialog or panel behind stays open

desktop.base: The same card as web at desktop density
notes: Today the mechanism is hand-rolled in parts/HoverCard.tsx and the panel is a sibling of the trigger. The 6px gap is padding on the panel's wrapper, never a margin on the panel, so the pointer never crosses a dead zone on the way in; the panel's own mouseenter cancels the pending close.
Both timers are cleared on unmount: the message list unmounts rows as it scrolls, and a timer that fires afterwards is a leak nobody sees.
z-index 80: above the menu panel layer (61) so a card opened over an open menu is readable, below the notification rail.
The card pops in (a short scale and fade from its trigger side); the catalogue's Replay plays it.
The status emoji does not go on the avatar here. Presence is a word on the line below, so the card never says the same thing twice.
Message and View profile are both secondary (ADR-9320). A card that opens because the pointer drifted has no commit action, so nothing in it is coral.
New in this spec: the job title and the local time. Today's card leaves both out because the platform serves no timezone; each line is drawn only when the profile carries it.
The mention pill's card (overlays/MentionProfileCard.tsx) is mounted once per screen and uses the same HoverCardSurface, so the two cards cannot drift apart.

keyboard.action: Opens after 380 ms, as hover does
Moves into the card's buttons
Closes immediately and stops propagation

mobile.alternative: A phone has no hover. Tapping an avatar or a name opens the person's profile sheet (a Bottom sheet): the same photo, name, title, presence, local time and status in the same order, with Message and View profile full width at the foot. Long-press stays free for the message's own actions.

icon-button.name: Icon button
icon-button.description: A single glyph that does one thing. The label is required: it is the tooltip on web and desktop and the accessibility label on mobile, so an icon is never unnamed.

active.description: Toggled on (e.g. the notification rail is open). Sets aria-pressed.

toggle.description: A toggle button (aria-pressed): pressing flips `active`, e.g. opening the notification rail or the thread panel. Off for one-shot actions — Close, Copy, Clear — which only give press feedback.

badge.description: Unread count drawn on the corner. 0 hides it.

avatar.description: { name, src?, identity?, presence? }: a person's face in place of the icon, filling the button (a profile button). `label` stays the name read aloud; the face is hidden from screen readers so it is not read twice. `icon` is still required and is not drawn while `avatar` is set.

onActiveChange.description: Called with `active` as the press leaves it: flipped. Only a toggle changes it; a one-shot button never calls it.

onPress.description: The button was pressed, toggle or not.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: Toggle buttons expose aria-pressed / accessibilityState.selected.
The badge count joins the label: "Notifications, 4 unread".
The web draws a 24px (sm) or 28px (md) target by default and grows to a finger's size on a touch screen; the phone draws 32 or 40pt and grows the touch area to 44pt without drawing more.
With `avatar`, the face is aria-hidden (web) / hidden from accessibility (phone): the button is named by `label` once, e.g. "Your profile: Priya Raman".

examples.name: Toggle — press it
examples.description: A toggle button: each press flips it on and off.

examples.name: Profile
examples.description: A person's face in place of the icon: the button that opens their profile, at the end of a top bar.

edgeCases.title: Badge over 9
edgeCases.handling: A corner badge caps at 9+ so it never covers the glyph.

edgeCases.title: A face in place of the icon
edgeCases.handling: With `avatar`, the face fills the button's own box at every size and platform (its own avatar sizes differ), takes the button's shape, and keeps the focus ring and badge. A photo that fails to load falls back to the initials, as Avatar does.

edgeCases.title: Touch on a laptop screen
edgeCases.handling: pointer: coarse raises the box to the mobile 40px so a finger on a Surface or touch Chromebook can hit it; the glyph stays the same size.

web.base: <button> with the label as aria-label and native title tooltip, inline styles over `t`; hover, press and focus from useInteraction; `active` through useControllable; corner Badge
notes: Pressing a toggle button (toggle: true) flips `active` (through useControllable, so the catalogue preview is interactive): the brand-soft fill and brand glyph fade in and out, and aria-pressed follows. A one-shot button's own action (open, send, close) stays with the caller.

keyboard.action: Activates
Shows the tooltip immediately (no hover delay)

desktop.base: The same <button> as web: inline styles over `t` at desktop density (28px box); the label is the native title tooltip
notes: Today the desktop draws 28px; that stays. The 24px hit minimum is met by the 28px box.
Pressing a toggle button (toggle: true) flips `active`: the brand-soft fill fades in over 120ms and aria-pressed follows.

notes: 40pt visible box (V2), with hitSlop to make 44pt.
Danger tone turns red only while pressed — a resting red icon reads as an error.
Tapping toggles `active` (accessibilityState.selected follows); the press scale eases back over 120ms.

gestures.action: Activates with a light haptic
Shows the label as a tooltip-style callout (iOS 17 / Android 14 pattern)

in-app-banner.name: In-app banner
in-app-banner.description: The foreground notification: AntFabric is open and in front, but you are somewhere else in it. A card that drops in below the status bar on a phone and sits top-right on web and desktop — never for the conversation already on screen.

title.description: The sender for chat; the event for a meeting or an agent.

context.description: Drawn after the title: the channel, the room. Empty for a direct message.

body.description: Two lines at most; the server's bounded preview.
body.sample: Can someone sanity-check the rollout plan before the 3pm train?

identity.description: The colour of the sender's initials when there is no `avatarSrc`. An agent is always drawn as one.

leading.description: avatar is the sender's face. tile is a glyph on a tile, for an event that has no sender (a meeting).

agent.description: The sender is an agent: its face, and no name colour.

lead.description: Words before the body: "Mentioned you", "Replied in a thread".

queued.description: How many more are waiting behind this one. They show one at a time; this says so.

replyable.description: A Reply button comes first, and opens the inline reply. Web and desktop only — on a phone a tap opens the conversation with the composer focused.

actions.description: The buttons under the text, after Reply: `{ key, label, icon?, variant?: "ghost" | "soft", dismiss? }`. A `dismiss` one puts the banner away when it is pressed (`onDismiss("action")`); each press reaches `onAction`.

replying.description: The inline reply is open. Web and desktop only — on a phone a tap opens the conversation with the composer focused.

error.description: Why the inline reply did not send. The draft stays in the box.

dismissed.description: Dismissed: × or Mark as read on web and desktop, a swipe up on the phone (the catalogue uses the grabber). The banner leaves and nothing is drawn.

onAction.description: An action under the text was pressed: the item itself, so a product switches on `action.key`.

notes: The banner sits in a polite live region that stays on the page (the web's root, the phone's role=status view), so what appears inside it is read as "Priya Raman in #platform-eng: …" — never assertive, and it never takes focus. On the phone the same words are also spoken through the screen reader's announcement call, because iOS has no live regions.
The kit has no auto-dismiss timer: the app owns it and must stop it while the banner has focus or the pointer is on it, and give a screen-reader user longer (WCAG 2.2.1).

Reply moves focus into the field, and Escape in the field closes the reply and keeps the draft without dismissing the banner (Escape elsewhere on the card dismisses it); focus goes back to Reply when the reply closes. These are the web's: the phone has no reply field.

edgeCases.title: The conversation is already on screen
edgeCases.handling: No banner. "On screen" is all three of: the window or tab is focused, the channel pane is actually drawn (not just the last-opened channel), and it is the same channel — or, for a thread reply, that thread's panel is open. Sitting in #platform-eng while a reply lands in a thread you have closed DOES get a banner. The inbox row is still written and the badge still counts.

edgeCases.title: Several arrive at once
edgeCases.handling: One banner at a time, each on screen at least 1.5 s before the next replaces it, with "+2 more waiting" so nothing is silently skipped. Three or more from one conversation inside 10 s collapse into one: "3 new messages" in #platform-eng. A reconnect backlog never replays as banners — it goes to the rail.

edgeCases.title: You are typing
edgeCases.handling: The banner never takes focus and never moves the composer or the keyboard. On a phone it sits under the status bar; on desktop and web it is top-right, away from the composer.

edgeCases.title: How long it stays
edgeCases.handling: 6 s, then it slides away. The timer pauses while the pointer is on it, while it has focus, while a reply is being typed, and while a finger holds it — a banner with a draft in it never disappears.

edgeCases.title: Inline reply fails, or you are offline
edgeCases.handling: The draft stays in the box and the banner stays up with the reason. Offline, the reply is refused before it is tried, with the composer's own sentence.

edgeCases.title: Reduced motion
edgeCases.handling: It fades in place (120 ms) instead of sliding; the swipe-to-dismiss still works and simply follows the finger.

edgeCases.title: Read somewhere else, or notifications paused
edgeCases.handling: Reading the conversation on another device removes the banner here at once. While notifications are paused, or "Show Notifications" is off, no banner is drawn; with the master switch off the rail entry is skipped too (applyNotification's existing rule).

edgeCases.title: Long names and 130% text
edgeCases.handling: The title truncates to one line with the channel truncating first; the body clamps at two lines. At 130% on a phone the card grows taller, never wider, and the time stays on the first line.

edgeCases.title: Liquid Glass and earlier iOS
edgeCases.handling: On iOS 26+ the banner sliding in under the status bar is glass, like the system's own. The desktop in-app card is ours and stays opaque on macOS 26. The glass follows the iPhone's own settings with no work from us, because the kit draws it with the system material (GlassView): Clear or Tinted (Settings → Display & Brightness → Liquid Glass) changes how much shows through, Reduce Transparency makes it frosted and nearly opaque while keeping its shape, and Increase Contrast adds a contrasting edge. The app subscribes to AccessibilityInfo 'reduceTransparencyChanged' only to adjust what it draws around the glass. iOS before 26 keeps the blur look. This happens live in the app as the person changes the setting.

web.base: <div role="status" aria-live="polite"> holding a card that slides in from the right with enter(): one <button> that opens it, an IconButton ×, Button actions and an inline reply <input> with Send; Escape dismisses, Enter sends. Inline styles over `t`; `dismissed`, `replying` and `replyText` kept in local state that follows the props. The app hosts it in its own top-right viewport, apart from the action toasts
notes: Shown only while this tab is visible AND focused (document.visibilityState === 'visible' && document.hasFocus()). A background tab raises the browser notification instead, and the tab title count changes either way.
With several AntFabric tabs open, only the most recently focused tab shows it — tabs agree through a BroadcastChannel so nobody gets the same banner three times.
Inline reply posts with a client_message_id, so a double Enter sends once.
In the catalogue, × and Mark as read set `dismissed` (the banner leaves), Reply toggles `replying` and the reply row fades in, and Send closes it again. The banner slides in from the right.

keyboard.action: Moves focus into the banner region and back out
Dismisses the focused banner
In the reply box: sends. On the banner: opens the conversation

desktop.base: The same card as web at desktop density; the app places it top-right under the title bar, above the content and never over the composer. Mod+Enter sends too (any Enter does)
notes: New on desktop: today a focused window gets the rail entry and the sound, and no banner at all. The banner uses the same isOnScreen() test the sound and the OS banner already use: window focused, channel pane drawn, and the same channel — or, for a thread reply, the same thread panel open.
When the window is not focused the OS notification is raised instead (shouldToast), never both.
The sound still plays on every message, including the channel on screen — the owner's rule of 2026-09-03 (ADR-0574).
Slides in from the right edge of the window; × and Mark as read set `dismissed`, Reply toggles `replying`.

keyboard.action: Moves focus into the banner region and back out
Dismisses the focused banner
In the reply box: sends

mobile.base: View (role status, polite live region) with a card that drops in with <Enter motion="drop">, drawn on GlassSurface (Liquid Glass on iOS 26+); a PanResponder swipe up follows the finger and dismisses, the grabber stands in for it, and a Dismiss accessibilityAction and the iOS escape gesture do the same; StyleSheet over useTheme(). The app hosts it over the root stack, with expo-notifications' handleNotification returning shouldShowBanner: false while the app is in front
notes: Fixes a gap: today every foreground notification raises the OS banner (shouldShowBanner: true), including one for the channel you are reading. The handler now asks the router for the open channel / thread and stays silent for it; everything else draws this banner instead of the OS one.
Sits below the status bar (safe-area top inset + 8pt), above the tab bar and the keyboard, and never moves the composer.
No inline reply on the phone: a tap opens the conversation with the composer focused, which is the reply.
Light haptic (selection) when it lands; no sound if the ringer switch is off.

iOS 26+: Liquid Glass — the surface is drawn through expo-glass-effect's GlassView (gated on its availability check; the material itself follows the device's Clear / Tinted, Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast settings). iOS 18 and earlier keep today's blur/opaque look.
Drops in from under the status bar. In the catalogue the grabber stands in for the swipe up and sets `dismissed`.

gestures.action: Opens the conversation, thread, meeting or approval
Dismisses it; the inbox row stays unread
Holds it on screen (the auto-dismiss timer pauses)

flows.title: A mention while you're elsewhere in the app drops in, and opens the conversation
Reply from the banner without leaving what you're doing

inline-banner.name: Inline banner
inline-banner.description: A notice that sits inside a pane, above the thing it is about, and stays as long as it is true: you are offline, you are previewing a channel, notifications are off, Fabric left you a note. Tone says who it is from — neutral is the state you are in, brand is Fabric.

tone.description: neutral: the state you are in. brand: the product's assistant did this — never use it for an outage, or the outage reads as the agent's. warning: something will go wrong if left (notifications off, storage nearly full). danger: something already failed and needs you.

icon.description: The glyph before the message. Left out, the tone's own: info for neutral and brand, triangle-alert for warning, circle-alert for danger; an empty string draws none.

title.description: Optional bold first line. Mobile footnote banners leave it out — a heading turns a footnote into a section.

message.sample: Showing what's on this device. New messages arrive when you reconnect.

actionLabel.description: At most one action; a second belongs on the screen the action opens.

actionVariant.description: primary only when the banner holds the view's one primary action (Join channel).

dismissible.description: Tips and announcements can be dismissed; a banner that states a fact (offline, archived, not a member) cannot, because it is true until it is not.

dismissed.description: Dismissed: the banner fades out. What the × does in the catalogue; in the app the banner unmounts, the pane closes the gap and onDismiss fires.

a11y.role: status (alert for danger on the phone)
notes: The title and message are spoken when the banner appears or its text changes. On the web that goes through the page's own announcer (polite, assertive for danger): the banner is not a live region itself, because one that arrives holding its text is not read. On the phone the screen reader's announcement call speaks it (iOS has no live regions) and the view carries role=status, or alert for danger.
Something that failed (danger) is announced at once; the other tones wait for a pause.

Tone is never the only signal — the icon and the words carry it. The dismiss button is named "Dismiss", not "×". Once dismissed the banner is inert on the web (its buttons leave the tab order) and hidden from the accessibility tree on both.

props.message: Review it before it goes to #platform-eng.

Ask Fabric to summarise any thread — type /summarise.

Recordings stay on this phone until they finish uploading.

edgeCases.title: Long message in a narrow pane
edgeCases.handling: The message wraps — it is never truncated, because the whole point is to be read. Under 420px of container width the web and desktop kits move the action below the text (a container query the static catalogue cannot draw); the phone always puts it below.

edgeCases.title: More than one banner wants the pane
edgeCases.handling: One banner per pane. The most urgent wins (danger, then warning, then neutral state, then brand); the rest wait. Offline outranks a Fabric tip; a tip never sits on top of an outage.

edgeCases.title: Dismissed on one device
edgeCases.handling: A dismissed tip stays dismissed for that person on every device (stored with their preferences, not only in localStorage). State banners cannot be dismissed, so there is nothing to sync for them.

edgeCases.title: Back online
edgeCases.handling: The offline banner leaves quietly once the resync lands — no "You're back online" toast. If messages were queued, one toast says what happened: "3 messages sent".

edgeCases.title: Notifications denied
edgeCases.handling: Desktop and mobile deep-link to the OS settings page (macOS System Settings, Windows ms-settings:notifications, iOS/Android app settings via Linking.openSettings). A browser that has denied permission will never prompt again, so the web banner explains the one manual step instead of offering a button that cannot work.

edgeCases.title: Brand is not a severity
edgeCases.handling: brand means Fabric did this. A brand-coloured banner about a network outage attributes the outage to the agent, so outages, failures and permission problems are neutral, warning or danger — never brand.

edgeCases.title: Screen reader
edgeCases.handling: Announced once when it appears (polite), never again on re-render. A banner whose action is the view's primary action (Join channel) is also reachable as the first control after the pane heading.

edgeCases.title: Dark mode
edgeCases.handling: Each tone uses its theme's soft fill (brand #382525, warning #372e1c, danger #362124) and the rim is mixed from the tone's own ink, so it reads as a layer on charcoal without a bright outline.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left
edgeCases.handling: The icon leads on the right; the action and the dismiss button sit at the left end.

web.base: A role="status" <div> that fades in with enter("fade"), with the kit's Button (sm) and IconButton (Dismiss); the × keeps `dismissed` inside and fades it out; inline styles over `t`
notes: Below 420px of container width (a container query, not the viewport) the action wraps under the text.
Browser-permission banners deep-link nowhere — a browser cannot open its own site settings — so they say where to click: "Click the lock in the address bar, then Notifications."

desktop.base: The same <div> as web, at desktop density
notes: Neutral is the WHITE card surface, not recessed (owner, 2026-09-03): on the warm page a cool recessed grey reads as a dirty patch, not a layer.
Its rim is border.subtle, the same as Card's — a heavier rim on the one box that is a notice reads as emphasis nobody asked for.
warning and danger are new in this spec; the desktop has neutral and brand today.
Permission banners open the OS page directly: x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.Notifications-Settings on macOS, ms-settings:notifications on Windows.
It fades in where it appears, and the × of a dismissible banner sets `dismissed`, which fades it out.

mobile.base: A View (role status, polite live region) with <Enter motion="fade">, the action under the message as the kit's Button (sm) and the kit's IconButton for Dismiss; dismissing fades it with Animated.timing
notes: Today's InfoBanner: a sunken strip (surface.muted), 12 × 8 padding, radius 8, a 16pt faint icon nudged 2pt down against the first line, one sentence and no heading. It has no bottom margin — the next SectionHeader owns the gap.
A title line is allowed for state banners (ConnectivityBanner has one); footnote banners leave it out.
The action sits under the message, aligned with the text; a phone is too narrow for text and a button side by side.
It fades in where it appears, and the × of a dismissible banner sets `dismissed`, which fades it out.

gestures.action: Runs it; the banner itself is not a button

The banner's action opens what fixes it

kbd.name: Keyboard shortcut
kbd.description: A shortcut, written once as Mod+Shift+K and drawn the way each OS writes it: ⌘⇧K on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+K on Windows and Linux.

notes: The glyphs are hidden from assistive tech and the shortcut is read in words ("Command K") from a visually hidden span: a <kbd> has no role to carry an aria-label.
The kit sets `aria-keyshortcuts` on the rows that draw a shortcut (Menu); a product that draws a Kbd beside its own control sets it there, with `ariaShortcut(keys, os)`.

edgeCases.title: Same shortcut, different OS
edgeCases.handling: Switch the OS on the Desktop tab: the component is given Mod+Shift+K once; macOS draws ⌘⇧K, Windows and Linux draw Ctrl+Shift+K.

edgeCases.title: Browser-reserved shortcut
edgeCases.handling: History back on desktop is ⌘[; in a browser that is the browser's own back, which works anyway. ⌘N (new message on desktop) opens a browser window, so the web app documents Mod+Alt+N instead.

edgeCases.title: Non-US keyboard layouts
edgeCases.handling: Shortcuts bind to KeyboardEvent.code for letters, so ⌘K works on AZERTY; punctuation shortcuts ([ ] /) bind to key, and Settings lets a person rebind them.

web.base: <kbd>, inline styles over `t`; glyphs from formatShortcut for the OS in usePlatform(), accessible name in words
notes: OS comes from navigator.userAgentData.platform (fallback navigator.platform). iPadOS reports as Mac — correct, its keyboards have ⌘.

desktop.base: The same <kbd> as web; ⌘⇧K glyphs with caps tracking on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+K on Windows and Linux
notes: OS comes from Tauri's @tauri-apps/plugin-os platform(), not the user agent.

mobile.alternative: Phones show no shortcut hints. On iPad with a hardware keyboard, shortcuts are registered as UIKeyCommands so holding ⌘ lists them — the system draws that, not us.

flows.title: Rebind a shortcut and every hint redraws

kpi-card.name: KpiCard
kpi-card.description: The headline KPI that leads a dashboard: its label and a Delta badge on top, the number large, a sentence saying what moved ("Up 4.4% on September") with a trending arrow, a note, and a trend bled into the card's foot, edge to edge. Several in a row make a dashboard's top; the compact version for a grid is a StatTile.

label.description: What the headline number is. It is the card's accessible name.

value.description: The number, drawn by MetricValue at its lg size. It eases to a new value.

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. The symbol and unit of the printed value are drawn smaller and fainter than the digits.

delta.description: The change, as a number the delta format prints: 0.044 is +4.4%. It is the badge and the sentence. Left out, the card has neither.

deltaFormat.description: The Delta's format (default a signed percent), for a change in points ("points") or a multiple. The sentence prints it without the sign: the word says it.

inverse.description: Down is good (open tickets, response time): the badge's colours swap. The sentence and the arrow still say the way the number went.

period.description: What the change is against, after the sentence: "on September" makes "Up 4.4% on September".

note.description: A line of context under the sentence. Left empty, there is none.

trend.description: Rows for the trend bled into the card's foot, one per period: [{ month: 4, mrr: 152400 }, …]. Used with `trendY`. It takes the card's full width and draws its fill to the bottom edge.

trendY.description: The field of each row that is the value.

loading.description: Grey lines the size of the label, the value and the note, from the kit's Skeleton, in place of the numbers. Screen readers hear "Loading Monthly recurring revenue" once.

a11y.label: The label; on the phone, "Monthly recurring revenue, $184,200, Up 4.4% on September, Forecast was $185,000"
notes: On the web the card is a labelled group, not a region landmark, so a row of cards adds no landmarks; the label, the value (once, plain), the sentence and the note read in that order. On the phone the whole card is one element with the sentence, so one swipe reads a card.
The badge beside the label is hidden from screen readers: the sentence says the direction, the size and the period once, after the value.
A figure too long for the card is written short on the web ($1.3B for $1,284,000,000) and the whole figure is the title of its box; the phone wraps it.
The trend is a labelled image ("Monthly recurring revenue, trend"): it is a picture of numbers, and the value above it is what carries the number.
Loading is a status named "Loading Monthly recurring revenue", announced once; the extra grey lines are hidden from screen readers.

examples.name: Open tickets, down is good
examples.description: Fewer is good: the badge is green though the arrow points down.

examples.name: Resolved by Fabric, in points
examples.description: A share changes in points, not in percent of a percent.

edgeCases.title: No comparison yet
edgeCases.handling: Without a `delta` there is no badge and no sentence; the note, if any, stays. It never says "Up 0%": a first period has nothing to be compared with.

edgeCases.title: No change
edgeCases.handling: Zero says "No change" with a flat dash, in the neutral ink: neither good nor bad.

edgeCases.title: A change that is not a number
edgeCases.handling: NaN reads "Change unavailable" with a flat dash and the badge shows an en dash. It is never drawn as 0%.

edgeCases.title: A long label
edgeCases.handling: The label wraps to a second line and the badge stays at the top right; the card grows to fit rather than cut its own name.

edgeCases.title: A trend with no rows
edgeCases.handling: An empty `trend`, or one with no `trendY`, draws no trend and the card keeps its own padding at the foot: no gap where the trend would have been.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section> drawn from the recipe: the label, Delta (badge), MetricValue (lg), a sentence with the trending Icon, a note; then a flush Sparkline in a measured <div>, outside the section's padding; Skeleton while loading
notes: Shipped from the data subpath. The trend is measured (a ResizeObserver) and drawn at the card's width: recharts takes a number, not a percentage.
A row of cards is the page's layout: a grid of auto-filled columns at least 240px wide.

desktop.base: The same Card and <section> as web, at desktop density

mobile.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a View, then a measured View holding a flush Sparkline (gifted-charts) at the card's width
notes: On the phone a row of KpiCards is a sideways snap row, each card about 82% of the screen so the next one peeks in. That is the screen's layout, not the card's: put the cards in a horizontal ScrollView with snapToInterval and the kit's own gap.
The Card is flat on the phone: the hairline border separates it, and `elevate` does not apply.

line-chart.name: LineChart
line-chart.description: One to five series as lines over time, in a card with a title, an optional headline number and a legend that turns series off. An optional flat fill under the first series, and a target line. The value axis follows the data (it does not start at zero), the tooltip follows the pointer or the finger, and "View as table" shows the same rows in Table.

headingLevel.description: The heading level of the card's title, 1 to 6, so the chart keeps the page's heading order: a card under an h2 is an h3, one under an h1 is an h2. The phone has one kind of header and reads it for nothing. The card is not a landmark: the figure inside is named by the summary.

data.description: Rows, one per point, in order: [{ month: 1777593600000, opened: 612, resolved: 580 }, …]. The same rows can feed a table, a stat and a bar chart.

x.description: The field of each row that is the category: a date or a word.

y.description: The field, or fields, that are the values: "mrr" or ["opened", "resolved"]. One to five; a sixth and after are not drawn , though "View as table" keeps every field. A value that is not a number leaves a gap.

title.description: The card's title. It names the figure on the page, and is the first words of what a screen reader hears.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: what it covers. Empty draws none.

headline.description: A number to lead with, under the title: { value, format, delta, deltaFormat, inverse, period }. It is a MetricValue (in the chart's format unless it names one), a Delta badge and what the change is against ("resolved in October"). Left out, the card has none.

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. The axis, the labels at the ends of bars, the tooltip, the summary and "View as table" all print through it, so they agree.

xFormat.description: The category's format, for a date: "month", "day", or options such as { type: "month", timeZone: "UTC" }. A timestamp under a date format is read as a point in time, so the summary reads as a trend. Left out, the category prints as it is.

labels.description: A field's name for people, for the legend, the tooltip and the table's headers: { opened: "Opened" }. A field with no entry prints its own name.

height.description: The plot's height, in px (points on the phone). The card is as wide as the space it is given.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when there are no rows. Say why: nothing yet and nothing matching a filter are different sentences.

emptyLine.description: One sentence under it: what to do about it.

loading.description: Grey bars of uneven heights in place of the plot, from the kit's Skeleton, and no "View as table". The header stays, so the card does not jump when the data arrives. Screen readers hear "Loading chart" once.

hidden.description: The series the legend has turned off, by field: ["resolved"]. Left out, the chart keeps its own, starting with every series on. Controlled when the app passes it with `onHiddenChange`.

onHiddenChange.description: A legend entry was pressed. Called with every series that is off now. The last series showing cannot be turned off, so pressing it calls nothing.

area.description: A flat fill under the first series: its colour at one opacity, never a gradient. Only the first is filled: two fills over each other mix into a colour neither series has.

marks.description: Each series gets its own dash pattern and marker shape besides its colour, in the plot and in the legend's key, so two series are never told apart by hue alone (WCAG 1.4.1). Markers are left off past 40 points. Left out, it is on for two or more series and off for one; `false` keeps plain lines where the product labels the series another way.

target.description: A reference line at this value: a goal, a limit. The value axis takes it in, so a target outside the data still shows.

targetLabel.description: What the target line says, at its right end: "Q4 target $180K". Empty draws a line with no words.

a11y.label: The summary: "Tickets opened and resolved, May to Oct: Opened rose from 612 to 769, highest in Oct; Resolved rose from 580 to 781, highest in Oct."
notes: The figure is named by the sentence core's `summarize` writes from the rows: dates read as a trend (rose, fell, held, and where it peaked), categories as highest and lowest. It is heard, not printed: in the light theme most series colours sit under 3:1 against the card, so the tooltip and "View as table" give the numbers without colour.
"View as table" is the other way in: the same rows in Table, with real headers. It is a Button, so it is reached by keyboard and named by what it will do.

With `marks` (on by default for two or more series), a series is told apart by its dash and marker as well as its colour (the first is solid with a round marker, the next dashed with a square, and so on), and the legend's key draws the same. With `marks={false}`, the tooltip and the table are the relief for series that are close in hue.

The legend says what it toggles: each entry is a button that is pressed while the series is on ("Resolved, pressed"), and an entry that is off is struck through and faint, not only dimmer. The last series showing cannot be turned off, so a chart is never blank because of a press.

On the web the plot is a stop for the arrow keys (recharts' accessibility layer): the tooltip moves point to point, and the plot draws a focus edge from the tokens while the keyboard is in it. The phone's plot is one image; the sentence and the table carry it.
The tooltip is drawn with `role="tooltip"` on the web and is never the only place a value is: the table has every one.

examples.name: Opened and resolved
examples.description: Two series, a fill under the first and a headline: the number the card leads with, its change and what it is against.

examples.name: MRR against a target
examples.description: One series with a goal: the target line and its label, and a value axis that takes the goal in.

examples.name: Five series
examples.description: The most a line chart draws. Each has its own colour from the palette, and the legend names every one.

examples.name: A series turned off
examples.description: `hidden` is the legend's state: Resolved is off, so the axis re-fits to Opened and the entry is struck through.

edgeCases.title: No rows
edgeCases.handling: An empty `data` draws the kit's EmptyState in the plot's place and says why (the title and line are props); the card keeps its header and has no "View as table" and no legend, since there is nothing to show or toggle. The figure's label says there is no data.

edgeCases.title: One point
edgeCases.handling: One row has no line to draw, so it is a dot (ringed in the card's colour, on the web; the phone's pointer still finds it). The summary says "Runs is 455": one value has no trend.

edgeCases.title: All zero
edgeCases.handling: A series that never leaves zero has no range to fit, so the axis reads 0 to 1 and the line lies along the bottom, not through the middle of a made-up scale. The summary says it held at 0.

edgeCases.title: Negative values
edgeCases.handling: A line may cross zero: the value axis runs under it and draws the zero rule with the others. A line of positive values never gets a negative axis, whatever air the scale adds.

edgeCases.title: More than five series
edgeCases.handling: A line chart draws the first five, on both kits (the phone's library draws five). The legend and the table hold the same five. A sixth is a different chart: a table, or a BarChart.

edgeCases.title: A long series name
edgeCases.handling: Names are the app's words, and a long one wraps in the legend and the tooltip rather than being cut; the legend's entries wrap onto a second line.

edgeCases.title: A target outside the data
edgeCases.handling: The value axis takes the target in, so a goal above every point still draws, with the line well under it, and the label stays inside the plot.

edgeCases.title: Loading
edgeCases.handling: Grey bars of uneven heights fill the plot and the card keeps its header. There is no legend, no table button and no summary yet. A screen reader hears "Loading chart" once.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section>: the title, an optional headline (MetricValue, Delta), the kit's Button for "View as table"; a ChartFrame (width measured, a fixed default on the server) holding recharts' ComposedChart with an Area for the fill and a Line per series; the Legend (toggle buttons) in the header beside the Button, as the reference dashboard has it
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is a dependency of the React kit and is reached only from there. The chart is handed an explicit width and height, never a responsive container.

Everything the chart reads from the tokens goes through `rechartsTheme(useChartTokens(), useReducedMotion())`, exported beside the chart: the dashed grid, the quiet axes, the crosshair, the target line, the series colours and the motion. A chart the kit does not ship is written with recharts and the same call: `<CartesianGrid {...theme.grid} /> <XAxis dataKey="week" {...theme.axis} /> <Tooltip {...theme.tooltip} content={…ChartTooltip…} />`, and it matches.
The lines draw in once over 600ms on the kit's ease-out and tween to new values (a series turned off, new rows); the tooltip glides between points over 150ms. Reduced motion turns all of it off.

The value axis does not start at zero: a line's height is not its value. core's `niceScale` rounds the ticks with a little air so a line never runs along the frame, and the phone prints the same ticks.

keyboard.action: Moves into the plot, then on to the legend's entries and "View as table"
In the plot: moves the tooltip to the next point
In the plot: moves the tooltip to the previous point
On a legend entry: turns the series off or back on

desktop.base: The same Card, recharts' ComposedChart and Legend as web, at desktop density
notes: The same `rechartsTheme()` as web. Hover is the pointer's, so the tooltip follows it; there is no press-and-hold.

keyboard.action: Moves into the plot, then on to the legend's entries and "View as table"
In the plot: moves the tooltip to the next point
In the plot: moves the tooltip to the previous point
On a legend entry: turns the series off or back on

mobile.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a View: the same header and Button, a ChartFrame measured by onLayout holding react-native-gifted-charts' LineChart (`data` to `data5`, `areaChart1` for the fill, `pointerConfig` for the tooltip); the Legend's toggles above the plot
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: gifted-charts and react-native-svg are reached only from there. The kit adds `expo-linear-gradient` as a peer, which gifted-charts loads at import.

`giftedTheme(useChartTokens())` is the chart tokens as gifted-charts' own props (the dashed rules, the quiet axes, the target line, the pointer, the series colours), exported beside the chart, so a chart the kit does not ship matches the ones it does.

gifted-charts' value axis is a range above an offset, so the kit converts core's `niceScale` into `yAxisOffset`, `maxValue`, `stepValue` and `noOfSections` (the target is `referenceLine1Position`, an absolute value): the same ticks as the web's.
The lines draw in unless the person reduces motion. Under react-native-web (the catalogue, `pnpm check`) gifted-charts' animation is off, because the values it animates with reach the DOM as text.

gestures.gesture: Press and drag along the plot
gestures.action: A dashed strip follows the finger and the tooltip card shows each series at that point; lifting the finger hides it
Turns the series off or back on

list-item.name: List item
list-item.description: One row in a list or a menu: a leading icon, tile or face, a title with an optional subtitle, and trailing detail, count, shortcut or chevron. Dense on web and desktop (30–36px), touch-sized on mobile (52–72pt).

subtitle.description: One line on web and desktop, up to two on mobile.

titleLines.description: How many lines the title may take before it truncates with an ellipsis. Left out, the title takes one line on web and desktop and two on mobile, which is how each platform draws a row today; a number sets the same limit on every platform.

leading.description: icon is a bare glyph on web and desktop (sidebar and menu rows) and sits in a tile on mobile, where every ListItem glyph has one. tile is a tile everywhere — the desktop FileRow's chip. avatar is a face.

avatar.description: { name, identity, src? } when leading is avatar.

tile.description: Tile and face size. 36 holds a 20pt glyph; 32 a 16pt glyph and a 16pt chevron (V2 Settings, ADR-9419).

detail.description: Trailing text: a time, a value ("Mentions only"), a size, a channel.

count.description: Unread mentions; draws the coral Badge. 0 hides it.

shortcut.description: A menu row's keyboard shortcut, written once as Mod+Shift+K.

href.description: The row navigates: with role link it is an <a href>, so middle-click and ⌘-click open a new tab. A plain click calls onPress and stays on the page when there is one.

chevron.description: The row opens another screen. Mobile and settings lists; never in a menu.

selected.description: The open conversation (a grey fill on web and desktop), the chosen option (a check), or a ticked row in a multi-select picker (role checkbox).

unread.description: Bold title in strong ink — the one signal that something is new without a mention.

destructive.description: Leave, delete, remove. Red title and glyph; the action still confirms.

divider.description: A hairline under the row, for card-less lists. The last row passes false.

role.description: link for a row that opens something (sidebar, inbox), menuitem in a menu, option in a single-choice picker, checkbox in a multi-select picker (Add people, Forward), button for an in-place action. A checkbox row draws the Checkbox's box at its trailing end, and the whole row is the control.

onSelectedChange.description: Called with `selected` as the press leaves it (a press toggles it).

onPress.description: The row was pressed. Opening what the row stands for is the caller's.

onLongPress.description: Acts on the row instead of opening it, usually by opening a menu of what can be done to it. Also offered as the row's "More actions" accessibility action. The web has no long press: its row offers a context menu.

notes: The accessible name joins title, subtitle, detail and the count in words: "Notifications, Mentions only", "design-crit, 3 mentions". A drawn shortcut is read from `aria-keyshortcuts` on the row (web); a leading Avatar is hidden from assistive tech, so the name is not read twice.

Role `link` with `href` is an <a href> (middle-click and ⌘-click open a new tab); without `href` the row is a plain button. The other roles (menuitem, option, checkbox) set that role on the button: the kit gives them no parent role and no arrow-key roving, so each is a Tab stop unless the parent supplies a menu or listbox.
A row with `onLongPress` on the phone lists it among its accessibility actions as "More actions", so a screen-reader user reaches it without the gesture.
Sidebar rows use aria-current="page" for the open conversation (link rows); picker rows (role option) use aria-selected.
Multi-select picker rows are role=checkbox with aria-checked (accessibilityState.checked on mobile); the box is hidden from assistive tech because the row already says it.
A disabled menu row stays focusable (aria-disabled) so a screen-reader user hears that it exists and why it is off.

examples.name: Multi-select row — press it
examples.description: A row in the Add people picker: the whole row ticks and unticks.
