edgeCases.title: Long names, long channels, long previews
edgeCases.handling: The title is one line with an ellipsis; the preview clamps at two and breaks anywhere, so a pasted URL cannot push the time off the row. The full text is the accessible name.

edgeCases.title: The message was deleted, or you left the conversation
edgeCases.handling: A deleted message's row reads "This message was deleted." and still opens the conversation at that spot. A row for a conversation you can no longer see opens nothing and says "That conversation is not in your list any more." — Clear still works.

edgeCases.title: Approval answered on another device
edgeCases.handling: The buttons are replaced live by the outcome and where it happened — "Approved on your phone · Fabric is posting it now". A press that loses the race gets the server's answer, not a second approval.

edgeCases.title: Approval expired
edgeCases.handling: Agent requests time out. An expired one says so and that nothing happened; it never shows buttons that can only fail.

edgeCases.title: Approving is slow, or pressed twice
edgeCases.handling: Approve shows its spinner the moment it is pressed and Decline locks, with an idempotency key on the request. Still spinning after 8 s: the row keeps waiting and the toast says "Still sending your approval…". A failure restores both buttons with "Couldn't send that. Try again."

edgeCases.title: Offline
edgeCases.handling: Mark as read and Clear apply at once and are sent when the connection is back; if the server refuses, the row comes back with "Could not mark that notification read. Try again." Approve and Decline are disabled with "You're offline. Approve when you're back." — an agent action is never queued.

edgeCases.title: Read on another device
edgeCases.handling: Reading the conversation anywhere clears the tint and the dot here through the same read-state event that clears the Dock badge, the tab title and the phone's icon badge.

edgeCases.title: Keyboard and screen reader
edgeCases.handling: Rows are reachable by Tab and arrow keys; the hover actions also mount on focus-within so a keyboard user gets them. On a phone the swipe actions are accessibility actions, because a screen reader cannot swipe.

web.base: <div role="listitem"> holding one full-width <button> that opens it (one accessible name for the row), Avatar with a kind badge or the glyph tile, and Mark as read / Clear buttons positioned over the row's end that fade in while `revealed`, hovered or focused within; Approve / Decline are Button. Inline styles over `t`, states from useInteraction; `read`, `revealed` and `approval` kept in local state that follows the props
notes: The row's actions mount on :hover AND :focus-within — mounting on hover alone puts nothing in the tab order for a keyboard user, and leaving them always mounted puts two buttons per row in it.
Opening a row marks it read on the server and navigates with the router (a real <a href> for ⌘-click into a new tab).

keyboard.action: Moves between rows (roving focus)
Opens the conversation, thread, meeting or approval
From a focused row, reaches Mark as read, then Clear

desktop.base: The same row as web at desktop density; the hover actions mount while the pointer is on the row or focus is inside it (React state, not CSS :hover), absolutely positioned so they never reflow the text
notes: Rows today lead with a 32px glyph tile (leading="tile"). The avatar lead is new; the owner should pick one for both apps.

Hover actions are mounted only while the pointer is on the row (React state, not CSS :hover), absolutely positioned so appearing never reflows the text. This spec adds focus-within as a second trigger.
A thread reply leads its preview with "Replied in a thread" — read from the same parentMessageId the click uses, so what the row says and where it goes cannot disagree.
Approve / Decline in the row is new: agent approvals have no rail affordance today.

In the catalogue, pressing a row sets `read` (the tint and dot fade) and toggles `revealed`, so the hover actions fade in; Mark as read sets `read`, and Approve / Decline set `approval`, which swaps the buttons for the outcome line.

keyboard.action: Moves between rows
Opens it
Reaches Mark as read and Clear

mobile.base: View (role listitem) with a Pressable row on an Animated.View: a PanResponder swipe left slides it open (Animated.timing on translateX, native driver; a full swipe clears) and Mark read / Clear slide in behind it with <Enter motion="slide-left">; both are also accessibilityActions. Avatar or the glyph tile, Button for Approve / Decline, StyleSheet over useTheme()
notes: No hover on a phone: the same two actions are a left swipe (Mark read, Clear — Clear is destructive and calls DELETE, not dismiss) and the accessibility actions menu.
Opening one swipe closes any other row that is open.
The unread tint runs edge to edge and fills the strip behind the swipe actions too, so the band stays one colour while the row is open.
A critical notification (priority=critical) swaps the coral tile and dot for the danger colour — today's behaviour, kept.
Approval rows have no phone screen yet; until they do the Approve / Decline buttons in the row are the only way to answer one on the phone.
In the catalogue a tap sets `read`; Mark read in the swipe strip (slides in from the right when `revealed`) sets it too and closes the strip.

gestures.action: Opens it
Reveals Mark read and Clear
Clears it

flows.title: Open a notification from the feed
Mark a row read, or clear it, without opening it

notification-schedule.name: Pause notifications
notification-schedule.description: Do not disturb, AntFabric's own: a Pause notifications menu (30 minutes to tomorrow morning, or a custom time), the pill that says notifications are paused and until when, and the note that quiet hours live on the server and so hold on every device.

surface.description: menu: the Pause notifications choices. pill: the line that shows while paused.

until.description: When the pause ends, in this device's local time: "9:00", "tomorrow, 9:00", "Mon 3 Nov, 14:30".

quietHours.description: The person's server-side quiet hours, or empty if none are set.

options.description: The choices, in order: `{ key, label, text?, detail?, until?, custom? }`. `label` is the row's accessible name (with `, detail` after it) and is drawn unless `text` is; `until` is what "Paused until" shows once the row is chosen; a `custom` row opens the picker instead of pausing.

note.description: The line under the choices. With `quietHours` it follows them; with neither, no row is drawn.
note.sample: Quiet hours are applied by the server, so they hold on every device.

onCustomDateChange.description: The picker's date field changed: what was typed. Given `customDate` too, the field is controlled; otherwise it keeps its own. Pause uses what is in the field.

onCustomTimeChange.description: The picker's time field changed: what was typed. Given `customTime` too, the field is controlled; otherwise it keeps its own. Pause uses what is in the field.

onPause.description: A choice was made: the chosen option's `key`.

onPausedChange.description: Called with `paused` as a choice (true, when it was not paused) or Resume (false) leaves it. Given `paused` too, the menu is controlled; otherwise it keeps its own.

notes: The choices are a labelled group of buttons, not a role=menu: the picker's fields and Pause are form controls, which a menu may not hold. Tab moves through them. A product that hangs it in a popover owns Escape and focus return.

The pill is a status that stays on the page, so its text changing ("Notifications paused until 9:00", or on again) is read. In the menu, a pause starting or its end moving is spoken through the page's announcer on the web and the screen reader's announcement call on the phone.
Times are read in words by the platform ("nine o'clock"); the menu items carry their detail in the label ("Until tomorrow, 9:00").

edgeCases.title: Paused on one device, paused on all
edgeCases.handling: Pause writes snoozed_until to the person's server-side notification preferences; the server stops sending pushes and banners to every device, and each client gets the change over the socket and shows the pill. Resuming anywhere resumes everywhere.

edgeCases.title: Time zones and travel
edgeCases.handling: "Until tomorrow" is 9:00 — or the start of their working hours — in the person's profile time zone, stored as an instant. Each device shows that instant in its own local time, so a phone in another time zone may read "until 4:30". Daylight-saving changes move nothing.

edgeCases.title: It ends while the app is closed, asleep or offline
edgeCases.handling: The server ends the pause, not a client timer. Each client also clears its pill locally at the time so it never shows "paused until 9:00" at 9:05, and re-reads on wake or reconnect. Offline, the menu is disabled with "You're offline. You can pause notifications when you're back."

edgeCases.title: What happens to what arrived while paused
edgeCases.handling: Nothing is lost and nothing is replayed: every notification is in the inbox, the badge and tab count keep counting, and resuming does not fire a burst of banners. Only new ones after resuming interrupt.

edgeCases.title: Someone needs you urgently
edgeCases.handling: In this version nothing breaks through a pause — no "notify anyway", no exceptions for meetings or approvals. The sender sees the person's paused state on their profile. Whether a meeting you host or an approval may break through is an open decision for the owner.

edgeCases.title: Custom time in the past or far away
edgeCases.handling: The Pause button is disabled until the time is later than now ("Pick a time later than now."), and the latest allowed is 7 days ahead; anything longer is turning notifications off, which is the Show Notifications switch.

edgeCases.title: Our pause and the OS's Focus
edgeCases.handling: Independent, and both apply: macOS/iOS Focus, Windows Do not disturb and Android DND hold what we send; our pause means we do not send. The pill only ever describes ours — we cannot read the OS's Focus state reliably, so we never claim it.

web.base: A labelled role="group" of <button> rows (Custom… carries aria-expanded), inline styles over `t`; hover, press and focus from useInteraction; `paused`, `until` and `custom` kept in local state that follows the props; the paused line and the picker fade in, the menu pops in (the pill fades) with enter(); the pill is a role="status" row with a Resume <button>
notes: Custom… is two text fields and an ink Button in the kit; in the app they become <input type="date"> and <input type="time">, so the picker is the browser's own and keyboard-accessible.

os-notification.name: OS notification
os-notification.description: A notification as the operating system draws it — macOS banner, Windows toast, GNOME card, the browser's own frame, iOS banner and Android heads-up — from one payload. We do not draw these; this spec is what we send, and what the person will see, on every surface.

appName.description: The app's name, which the OS draws in its header (the browser's, Windows', GNOME's, Android's); its first letter is the small mark.

origin.description: The web origin a browser names beside the app. "" names none.

title.description: The bold line. For chat it is the sender's name; for a meeting or an agent it is the event ("Design crit starts in 5 min").

body.description: The server's bounded preview (140 characters, never the whole message).
body.sample: Can someone sanity-check the rollout plan before the 3pm train? Staging is green.

sender.description: Whose face goes on the banner (iOS/macOS communication notification, Android/Windows/web large icon).

identity.description: The colour of the sender's initials when there is no `avatarSrc`. An agent is always drawn as one.

context.description: macOS/iOS subtitle, Android sub-text, Windows attribution. Empty for a DM.

leading.description: avatar is the sender's face. tile is the app's own icon, for an event that has no one to show (a meeting).

agent.description: The sender is an agent: its face, and no badge.

lead.description: Words before the body: "Replied in a thread".

actions.description: The banner's buttons, at most two: `{ key, label, icon?, reply?, rest? }`. The one with `reply` opens the inline reply and its text comes back with the press (Windows always shows that field). `rest` marks the ones the OS shows before the banner is expanded: Windows always, the browser once expanded; macOS and GNOME show them all when expanded, and iOS lists them in the long-press menu with their `icon`.

preview.description: false is the person's "Hide message previews" setting: the server sends "New message" and no body, sender or channel.

grouped.description: How many more are stacked under this one from the same conversation (iOS threadIdentifier, Android group, Windows group, web tag).

expanded.description: The state the OS reveals the actions in: hover on macOS, long-press on iOS, the expand chevron on Android and GNOME, the notification centre on the web.

reply.description: An inline reply typed into the notification itself.

replyText.description: What the person has typed into the inline reply.

onClose.description: The banner's close button: the Mac's (drawn once the banner is expanded) and the × on Windows, Linux and the browser.

onSettings.description: Windows: the ⋯ button, the app's notification settings.

notes: The OS reads it: VoiceOver and Narrator speak title, subtitle and body, so the title must make sense alone ("Priya Raman", not "New").
The face is decoration; who sent it is always in the words.
Every action label is a verb that works out of context: "Reply", "Mark as read", "Join", "Approve".

edgeCases.title: Previews hidden (our setting or the lock screen)
edgeCases.handling: With "Hide message previews" on, the server sends "New message" with no body, sender or channel — on every device, because the setting is the person's, not the phone's. Separately, iOS "Show Previews: When Unlocked" and Android's lock-screen visibility hide our text on a locked device; we never work around either. Grouping still works because the thread id is not text.

edgeCases.title: A burst from one conversation
edgeCases.handling: One conversation is one stack: iOS threadIdentifier and Android setGroup are the channel id, with a summary ("+3 more from #platform-eng"); macOS threadIdentifier the same; Windows Group = channel, Tag = notification id; the web `tag` = channel id so the browser replaces rather than stacks. The sound plays once per 2.5 s however many arrive.

edgeCases.title: Reply sent from the notification
edgeCases.handling: Each reply carries a fresh client_message_id so a retry de-duplicates upstream, and a press is remembered per (notification, action) so Android delivering it to both the listener and the headless task sends once. Success marks the conversation read, removes the notification and updates the badge. Failure leaves the notification where it is with "Your reply wasn’t sent. Open AntFabric to send it." — silently dismissing it would read as sent. An empty reply is not sent.

edgeCases.title: Sending the reply
edgeCases.handling: The field locks and the send button spins until the server answers; on a phone with no session yet (a cold background launch) the session is restored first. Nothing is queued: offline, the reply fails and stays in the tray.

edgeCases.title: The message was deleted before the tap
edgeCases.handling: A delete retracts the notification (a silent push / socket event removes it from the tray and Notification Center by id). If the tap wins the race, the conversation opens at the place the message was, which reads "This message was deleted" — never an error screen.

edgeCases.title: The destination has no screen on this device
edgeCases.handling: Agent approvals, agent runs, work items and projects have no phone screen yet. The tap opens nothing and shows a toast with the app's existing sentence, e.g. "Agent approvals are not available on the phone yet." The notification stays unread so it is still waiting on desktop. The phone deliberately does not say "Open this on desktop" today (it would be a claim about another app) — that wording is the owner's call.

edgeCases.title: Read somewhere else
edgeCases.handling: Reading the conversation on any device retracts the banner everywhere: dismissNotificationAsync on the phone (driven by a silent push), removeDeliveredNotifications(withIdentifiers:) on macOS, ToastNotificationHistory.Remove(tag, group) on Windows, registration.getNotifications({ tag }) → close() on the web. A stale banner is a lie about what needs you.

edgeCases.title: Focus, Do Not Disturb and paused notifications
edgeCases.handling: The OS decides: macOS/iOS Focus, Windows Do not disturb / Focus Assist and Android DND hold banners silently in the notification centre. Meetings starting and approvals are sent as time-sensitive (iOS interruptionLevel timeSensitive, Android category CALL/REMINDER) so a person can let them through. When the person pauses notifications in AntFabric, the server sends nothing at all — see Notification schedule.

edgeCases.title: Approve from a locked phone
edgeCases.handling: Approve and Decline are registered with authenticationRequired (iOS) / setAuthenticationRequired (Android 12+), so Face ID or the passcode runs before the action does. Reply and Mark as read do not need it.

edgeCases.title: Window hidden in the tray, tab in the background, app killed
edgeCases.handling: Desktop: closing the window hides it, the socket stays up, document.hasFocus() is false, so the banner goes out (ADR-0379); clicking it reveals the window. Web: a background tab can raise one while it is open; with every tab closed only a Push API subscription can, and only while the browser itself runs. Mobile: APNs/FCM deliver with the app killed, and a cold-start tap is read once from getLastNotificationResponseAsync and then cleared, so it never replays.

edgeCases.title: Windows: small taskbar buttons and badges
edgeCases.handling: With small taskbar buttons (Windows 10) or taskbar badges switched off (Windows 11) the overlay badge is not drawn at all, so the toast and the Action Center count are the only signal. Nothing here may depend on the badge being seen — see App badge.

edgeCases.title: Long text, emoji and right-to-left names
edgeCases.handling: The server caps the preview at 140 characters and strips markdown; the OS truncates from there. A name in Arabic or Hebrew is sent as written and the OS lays it out right-to-left; we never pad or reorder it.

edgeCases.title: Liquid Glass and earlier iOS / macOS
edgeCases.handling: The OS draws these, so the version on the device decides: Liquid Glass on iOS 26+ and macOS 26+, the blur card before. Pick either version in the catalogue's top bar to compare. Windows, Linux, Android and the browser never change.

edgeCases.title: The device's Liquid Glass settings
edgeCases.handling: iOS and macOS draw these banners, so the person's own settings apply with no work from us: Clear or Tinted (iOS 26.1+ / macOS 26.1+), Reduce Transparency (frosted, nearly opaque) and Increase Contrast (a contrasting edge). This happens live as the person changes the setting.

web.base: A drawing of Chrome's own notification frame: a `<button>` for the banner and one per action, inline styles over `t`, the face from Avatar, hover and focus from useInteraction, rising in with enter("rise"). What the app uses is the Web Notifications API — ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification() for pushes (Push API + VAPID), new Notification() only while a tab is open — and the browser draws it.
notes: Chrome, Edge and Safari on macOS and Windows hand the notification to the OS, so there it looks like the macOS banner or Windows toast with the browser's icon and "app.antfabric.com" underneath. This frame is what Chrome draws itself (Linux, ChromeOS, and macOS with native notifications off).

No inline reply: `actions` with type 'text' is not supported in any shipping browser. Action buttons (max 2) work only on Chromium-based browsers with a service worker; Safari and Firefox show the body and nothing else, so a click that opens the right conversation is the whole contract.
`tag` is the channel id and `renotify: true` — a burst in #platform-eng replaces one banner instead of stacking six; `data` carries ids only, never the preview.
Never asked for on page load: see Permission prompt. Without permission, the tab title count and favicon dot (App badge) are the only signal.
Pressing the notification toggles `expanded` (Chrome's action buttons fade in); it rises in from the bottom-right corner, where Chrome draws its own.

keyboard.action: Activates the focused banner — the browser and OS own focus here, not the page

desktop.base: A drawing of the macOS banner, the Windows toast or the GNOME card, picked by usePlatform().os: `<button>`s for the banner, close and actions, an `<input data-af-input>` for the inline reply, inline styles over `t`, the face from Avatar, hover and focus from useInteraction, Liquid Glass through glass() on macOS 26, sliding in with enter("slide-left"). What the app calls is the Tauri `notify_show` command → UNUserNotificationCenter on macOS (src-tauri/src/notify_click.rs), and tauri-plugin-notification (WinRT toast on Windows, notify-rust / libnotify on Linux) elsewhere.
notes: Raised only when the window is NOT focused (shouldToast) — so it is also what reaches you when AntFabric is closed to the tray. The rail entry is written either way.

Today the title is one line, "Priya Raman · #platform-eng"; this spec splits it — sender is the title, the channel is the macOS subtitle / Windows attribution — so the name is never the part that truncates.

macOS: the request identifier IS the notification id, so a re-post replaces rather than duplicates, and a click returns that id through `notification:open` to the same openNotification the rail row runs.

Gap: no desktop banner has actions today. macOS needs a UNNotificationCategory `chat_message` with a UNTextInputNotificationAction `reply` and an action `mark_read` — the same identifiers the phone uses — handled in did_receive_response.

Gap: Windows and Linux go through tauri-plugin-notification, which has no click or action callback on desktop at any layer. Clicks, Reply and Mark as read need a WinRT ToastNotification activation handler (with an AUMID and a Start-menu shortcut) and notify-rust's wait_for_action on Linux.
The OS banner carries the OS sound; the in-app sound is throttled to one per 2.5 s on top of it (SOUND_THROTTLE_MS).
macOS 26+ (Tahoe): banners are Liquid Glass, drawn by macOS. macOS 15 and earlier: the vibrancy blur card. Windows and Linux are unchanged.

In the catalogue, pressing a banner toggles `expanded` — the body opens to eight lines and, on macOS and GNOME, the actions fade in (Windows always shows them). Reply opens the inline reply field and Send fires onAction(reply, text). Banners slide in from the right edge of the screen.

keyboard.action: macOS: with VoiceOver on the banner, opens it

mobile.base: A drawing of the iOS banner (with its long-press menu) or the Android heads-up, picked by useTheme().os: Pressables for the banner and actions, a TextInput for the inline reply, StyleSheet over useTheme() tokens in the system face, the face from Avatar, GlassSurface on iOS 26, dropping in with <Enter motion="drop">. What the app uses is expo-notifications — APNs / FCM push from notification-service, category `chat_message` (Reply with text input, Mark as read), Android channel `default` = "Messages and alerts", importance MAX, lock-screen PUBLIC.
notes: Both actions are `opensAppToForeground: false`: iOS wakes the app in the background, Android runs the headless task `antfabric-notification-action` even with the app killed (services/notificationActions.ts).
The payload is ids and a destination only; the title and body are the server's words, drawn and discarded. Nothing quotable is written to `content.data`, which the OS keeps.

Gap: the sender's face needs a Notification Service Extension donating an INSendMessageIntent on iOS (communication notification), and a native module for Android's MessagingStyle / large icon — expo-notifications can set neither per notification. Until then iOS shows the app icon and Android shows no large icon.
Android action labels are drawn as written ("Reply", "Mark as read") from Android 12; Android 7–11 upper-cases them (REPLY, MARK AS READ).
Today's Profile switch still says "Notifications don't show content. Open the app to see it" — no longer true since banners carry the server's words (2026-09-15). That subtitle needs rewriting.
iOS 26+: notifications and the lock screen are Liquid Glass — drawn by iOS, so the app has nothing to build; this preview shows what people will see. iOS 18 and earlier: the blur card.
Pressing the banner toggles `expanded`: on iOS the long-press menu pops in under it, on Android the chevron flips and the body opens. Reply opens the inline reply field. Both drop in from the top.

pagination.name: Pagination
pagination.description: Where you are in a long list and the way to move: a summary of the rows on show, previous and next, and the page numbers, with the page you are on filled. A Table draws one under itself when it has more rows than a page; a list or a feed can use it alone.

page.description: The page on show, counted from 1. A value outside the pages is brought back inside them.

total.description: How many rows there are in all. Gives the summary ("Showing 6–10 of 48") and, with `pageSize`, the page count.

pageCount.description: How many pages there are, for a list whose total is not known: the summary then reads "Page 3 of 7". Left out, it is worked out from `total` and `pageSize`.

pageSize.description: Rows a page. Changeable when `pageSizes` is given.

pageSizes.description: The choices of rows a page ([10, 25, 100]): a labelled "Rows per page" Select beside the summary. Left out, the page size is not the reader's to change.

jump.description: A labelled "Go to page" Select of every page, to go straight to one. Meant for up to a few hundred pages; past twelve it is searchable.

onPageSizeChange.description: A choice was made in the page-size Select. Called with the rows a page; the pager goes back to page 1 with it.

compact.description: The summary, previous and next, with no page buttons and a shorter summary ("6–10 of 48"). For a narrow place; the phone's Table uses it.

onPageChange.description: A page button, previous or next was pressed. Called with the page it goes to, counted from 1. It is never called for the page already on show.

a11y.label: "Pages"; previous and next are "Previous page" and "Next page", the pages are "Page 3" with the current one marked aria-current (web) or selected (phone)
notes: The summary is a polite live region, so paging announces "Showing 6–10 of 48" without moving focus.

On the first page previous is disabled, on the last next is. When the button a keyboard user pressed becomes disabled, focus moves to the current page button (or, in a compact pager, to the other arrow) so they keep their place.
`pageSizes` and `jump` are labelled Selects ("Rows per page", "Go to page").
The gap between page numbers is hidden from screen readers.

edgeCases.title: One page
edgeCases.handling: Previous and next are both disabled and one page is drawn, filled. A Table draws no Pagination at all while its rows fit one page; a list that always shows one should do the same.

edgeCases.title: A page that is not there
edgeCases.handling: A `page` below 1 or past the last is brought back inside the pages, so a list that shrank under the person (a filter that left 2 pages) still shows a real page. The summary follows it.

edgeCases.title: Hundreds of pages
edgeCases.handling: The slots stay seven: the first, the last, the current page and one either side. Press the last to jump to it.

notes: Seven page slots at most: past seven pages the first, the last and the neighbours of the current one are drawn with a gap between, so the pager is always the same width.
The current page is marked on its button (aria-current), and each page button is named "Page 3"; this relies on the kit's Button passing `aria-label` and `aria-current` to its element.

period-compare.name: PeriodCompare
period-compare.description: This period against the last: both totals, this one large with a change badge and what it is against, beside a line chart that draws this period solid with a flat fill and the last one dashed, thinner and in a quiet grey. The totals sit beside the chart on the web and the desktop, and in a row above it on the phone. "View as table" shows both periods' rows in Table.

data.description: Rows, one per point of the period, in order: [{ day: "Mon", thisWeek: 64, lastWeek: 58 }, …]. The same rows can feed a table and a line chart. A value that is not a number leaves a gap, and counts as 0 in a total.

x.description: The field of each row that is the category: a day, a date or a word.

current.description: The field that holds this period's values. Its line is solid, in the first series colour, with a flat fill under it.

previous.description: The field that holds the last period's values. Its line is dashed and thinner (`chart.previousW`), in `chart.previous`, with no fill.

title.description: The card's title. It names the figure on the page, and is the first words of what a screen reader hears.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: what it covers. Empty draws none.
subtitle.sample: This week against last, a day at a time

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. The two totals, the axis, the tooltip, the summary and "View as table" print through it, so they agree.

xFormat.description: The category's format, for a date: "month", "day", or options such as { type: "month", timeZone: "UTC" }. A timestamp under a date format is read as a point in time, so the summary reads as a trend. Left out, the category prints as it is.

labels.description: A field's name for people, over its total, in the tooltip and in the table's headers: { thisWeek: "This week" }. A field with no entry prints its own name.

notes.description: A line under each total, by field: what the period is. Left out, the total has none.

inverse.description: Down is good (spend, churn, response time): the badge's colours and its spoken "good" or "bad" swap, the arrow does not.

period.description: What the change is against, after the badge. The badge is this period's total against the last one's, never a prop: it cannot disagree with the two totals beside it.

height.description: The plot's height, in px (points on the phone). The card is as wide as the space it is given.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when there are no rows. Say why: nothing yet and nothing matching a filter are different sentences.

emptyLine.description: One sentence under it: what to do about it.

loading.description: Grey lines where the totals go and grey bars in place of the plot, from the kit's Skeleton, and no "View as table". The header stays, so the card does not jump when the data arrives. Screen readers hear it once.

a11y.label: The summary: "Tickets resolved by Fabric: This week 412 against Last week 371, up 11.1%. This week: highest Thu (75), lowest Sun (34); Last week: highest Wed (66), lowest Sun (31)."
notes: The figure is named by the sentence core's `summarizeCompare` writes from the rows: both totals, the change, and each period's best and worst point. It is heard, not printed: both totals sit beside the plot with their names, so colour is never the only way in. Dashed against solid is the second way to tell the two lines apart.
On the phone each total is one accessible element ("This week, Oct 19 to 25, 412, up 11.1% vs last week"), and the key's line and the badge are not read separately.
The change is the badge's own sentence ("Up 11.1%, good"), which Delta says; a last period of nothing says "Change unavailable" and not 0%.
"View as table" is the other way in: both periods, point by point, in Table with real headers.
With `inverse` a rise reads "Up 11.1%, bad", in words as well as colour. On the web the totals column wraps above the plot when the card is too narrow to leave the plot room.

edgeCases.title: No rows
edgeCases.handling: An empty `data` draws the kit's EmptyState in the plot's place and says why (the title and line are props); the card keeps its header, and has no totals and no "View as table", since there is nothing to total or show. The figure's label says there is no data.

edgeCases.title: A last period of nothing
edgeCases.handling: A change is a share of what it is against, and nothing has no share. When the last period totals 0 the badge reads "Change unavailable" with an en dash, the screen reader's sentence leaves the change out and does not say 0%, and both lines and totals are drawn as they are.

edgeCases.title: One point
edgeCases.handling: One row has no line to draw: each period is a ring in its own colour (this one blue, the last one grey), and the totals are those two numbers.

edgeCases.title: Loading
edgeCases.handling: Three grey lines the size of a total, a note and a badge fill the column of totals and grey bars of uneven heights fill the plot; the card keeps its header. There is no table button and no summary yet. A screen reader hears "Loading totals" and "Loading chart" once each.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section>: the title and "View as table" (Button); a row of a column of two <figure> totals (MetricValue, Delta) and a ChartFrame holding recharts' ComposedChart: the same Area and Line the LineChart draws, the last period's Line dashed and thinner
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is reached only from there. The plot is LineChart's own (the kit's `RechartsLines`), so the grid, axes, tooltip, crosshair and motion are the same, and the legend is gone because the two totals are the key: each has a short line in its series' colour, solid or dashed as the chart draws it.
The two periods share one value axis, which does not start at zero (a line's height is not its value), so a gap between them is the gap in the numbers.

The change is worked out from the two totals: (this less last) over last, printed as a signed percent in a Delta badge. A last period of nothing has no change to say, so the badge reads "Change unavailable".
The lines draw in once over 600ms on the kit's ease-out, and the totals ease to new numbers (MetricValue). Reduced motion turns both off.
The column of totals is `chart.sideW` wide with a rule on its right; below that width the card is narrower than the chart needs and the plot gives way first.

In the plot: moves the tooltip to the next point
In the plot: moves the tooltip to the previous point

notes: The same chart as the web's. Hover is the pointer's, so the tooltip follows it.

permission-prompt.name: Notification permission prompt
permission-prompt.description: The soft-ask before the operating system's own permission dialog, and what to say after it. It explains why, asks from a click, and when the answer was no it says exactly where the switch is on this OS — because most platforms only ask once.

permission.description: The OS's answer. default = never asked. Windows and Linux have no prompt, so default there reads as on.

origin.description: The site the browser's permission prompt names, drawn in the address-bar picture of a blocked tab. "" draws none.

presentation.description: card is the prompt on its own (a settings row, a banner in a pane). sheet is how the phone presents the soft-ask: the prompt IS the bottom sheet — full width, top corners rounded, a grab handle — never a card inside another sheet.

onAllow.description: Runs the OS request — from this click, never on load.

onQuiet.description: iOS provisional authorisation: deliver quietly to Notification Center without asking.

onCheckAgain.description: "Check again" in a tab whose notifications are blocked: the app re-reads Notification.permission and passes the new `permission`.

notes: The title is a heading; the state is said in words, never only by the tile colour.
Settings paths are written out ("System Settings → Notifications → AntFabric") so a screen-reader user can follow them without the picture.

examples.name: Ask first (iOS)
examples.description: iOS asks once; Deliver quietly uses provisional authorisation.

examples.name: Presented as a sheet (iOS)
examples.description: How the phone shows the soft-ask: the prompt is the bottom sheet itself, rising over the dimmed screen.

edgeCases.title: Asked once, on purpose — never on load, never on resume
edgeCases.handling: The OS request runs only from the Turn on click. The soft-ask appears after the first DM or mention arrives, or from Settings — not on the first screen after sign-in. Not now hides it for 14 days; after a third Not now it lives only in Settings. On the phone a resume re-reads the answer and never asks (the 59-ask loop).

edgeCases.title: Android: denied twice is denied for good
edgeCases.handling: After a second refusal Android stops showing its dialog (canAskAgain = false) and a request answers denied instantly. nextPushStep() then returns settings: the card swaps Turn on for Open Settings, and coming back with notifications allowed turns them on without another tap.

edgeCases.title: iOS: provisional (quiet) delivery
edgeCases.handling: Deliver quietly requests provisional authorisation: no dialog, notifications go silently to Notification Center, each with Keep and Turn Off. Status then reads provisional, and the Profile switch shows "Delivered quietly" with Turn on banners — which asks the real question then.

edgeCases.title: Changed in system settings while the app is open
edgeCases.handling: Re-read on focus (web: permissions.query change event; desktop: window focus; phone: AppState active). A switch in the app that still claims on after notifications were turned off in Settings is the bug this prevents.

edgeCases.title: Dev builds and the wrong sender on Windows
edgeCases.handling: pnpm tauri dev is not a bundled app, so macOS's UNUserNotificationCenter refuses it and banners fall back to the plugin path; on Windows an unpackaged dev binary has no AppUserModelID and its toasts appear from "Windows PowerShell". The installer registers the AUMID and a Start-menu shortcut; neither is a permission problem and the card must not say it is.

edgeCases.title: Browsers that cannot, and private windows
edgeCases.handling: Safari on iPhone and iPad supports web push only for a site added to the Home Screen (iOS 16.4+); Firefox private windows and some embedded webviews have no Notification at all. Those read unsupported, with what to do; the tab title count and favicon dot still work.

edgeCases.title: Several tabs or windows
edgeCases.handling: Permission is per origin (web) and per app (desktop): granting in one tab grants every tab, and the cards in the others disappear on the change event. Only the focused tab shows the soft-ask.

edgeCases.title: Granted, but nothing arrives
edgeCases.handling: Send a test notification posts a real one through the same path. If it does not appear the card says the likely cause for this OS — Focus / Do not disturb, the browser's own notification switch in System Settings, or (phone) a missing push token, which is retried on the next resume.

edgeCases.title: Soft-ask nested inside another sheet
edgeCases.handling: Never put the card inside a BottomSheet: two surfaces, two sets of corners, and a fixed-width card that overflows the sheet's gutter. Use presentation: "sheet", which makes the prompt the sheet — full width, top corners only, its own grab handle — and leaves the home-indicator space to the screen.

edgeCases.title: Liquid Glass and earlier iOS
edgeCases.handling: As a sheet on iOS 26+, the soft-ask floats inset as a Liquid Glass sheet. The glass follows the iPhone's own settings with no work from us, because the kit draws it with the system material (GlassView): Clear or Tinted (Settings → Display & Brightness → Liquid Glass) changes how much shows through, Reduce Transparency makes it frosted and nearly opaque while keeping its shape, and Increase Contrast adds a contrasting edge. The app subscribes to AccessibilityInfo 'reduceTransparencyChanged' only to adjust what it draws around the glass. iOS before 26 keeps the blur look. This happens live in the app as the person changes the setting.

web.base: <div role="region"> card with an <h2> title, inline styles over `t`; Button actions; `permission` kept in local state that follows the prop, so Turn on shows the on state at once; pops in with enter(); the blocked-in-browser hint is drawn aria-hidden. The app runs Notification.requestPermission() inside onAllow and watches navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'notifications' })
notes: Shown in the notification rail and once as a dismissible card on the home screen after the first DM or mention arrives — never as a prompt on page load.

The OS prompt is requested only from the Turn on click: Safari and Firefox refuse a request without a user gesture, and Chrome switches a site that prompts on load to its quiet UI (a crossed bell in the address bar) that most people never see.
Denied cannot be undone from the page — no API reopens the prompt. The card says where the switch is and offers Check again, which re-reads Notification.permission.
In the catalogue, Turn on notifications sets `permission` to granted (the browser would ask first), so the prompt turns into the on state with Send a test notification. The card pops in.

keyboard.action: Activates the focused button

desktop.base: The same card as web at desktop density, its copy and actions per OS from usePlatform() (macOS asks; Windows and Linux read as on). The app runs UNUserNotificationCenter requestAuthorization (macOS) or tauri-plugin-notification inside onAllow, and opens x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.Notifications-Settings.extension / ms-settings:notifications from onOpenSettings
notes: Today macOS asks at startup with no explanation, and the answer is cached; this card moves that ask behind the soft-ask on first launch, because macOS also asks only once.
Windows: unpackaged apps are allowed by default; there is nothing to ask. The card only appears in Settings, as "Notifications are on" with a test button.
Linux: no permission model. If no notification server is running (some tiling setups), notify-rust fails silently; the test button is how a person finds out.
Linux has no settings page to open, so when notifications are off there the card offers Send a test notification instead of a settings button.
The rail's own switches (Notification sound, Show Notifications) are a separate, per-machine setting and are not this permission.
Turn on notifications sets `permission` to granted in the catalogue (macOS would ask first); the card pops in.

keyboard.action: Activates the focused button

mobile.base: View (role region) over GlassSurface (Liquid Glass for the sheet on iOS 26+), StyleSheet over useTheme(); full-width Buttons in a column; <Enter> slides the sheet up and pops the card. The app calls expo-notifications requestPermissionsAsync({ ios: { allowProvisional } }) from onAllow / onQuiet and Linking.openSettings() from onOpenSettings
notes: Today the phone asks the OS the moment the notification socket first connects, with no soft-ask. This sheet goes in front of that ask, once per install.

Keep the rule from 2026-09-28: a foreground resume only READS the permission (registerPushDevice({ ask: false })), never asks. Asking on resume pauses and resumes the app, which is the resume event — it looped 59 times in 7.6 s and jammed Expo's permission queue.
Android 13+ needs the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission; Android 12 and earlier are allowed by default, so the sheet skips straight to granted there.
Coming back from Settings with notifications allowed turns the Profile switch on without a second tap (awaitingSettings).

iOS 26+: Liquid Glass — the surface is drawn through expo-glass-effect's GlassView (gated on its availability check; the material itself follows the device's Clear / Tinted, Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast settings). iOS 18 and earlier keep today's blur/opaque look. Only the sheet presentation takes glass; the card stays opaque so the explanation reads cleanly wherever it sits.

Turn on notifications sets `permission` to granted in the catalogue (the OS would ask first). The card pops in; the sheet presentation pops too, because one template root carries one entrance — the kit slides the sheet up.

gestures.action: Same as Not now

Turned off: say where the switch is, and take them there

popover.name: Popover
popover.description: A panel that hangs from the control that opened it: a menu, a short form, a list, a card of anything. It floats above the page in the overlay layer (whatever the page's overflow), flips to the other side where there is no room, follows its trigger as the page scrolls, and closes on Esc and a press outside, giving focus back to the trigger. Not for a decision that blocks the page (Dialog) or a side panel (Sheet).

content.description: What the panel holds. With `bare`, content that is already a card (a Menu) is drawn without a second one round it.

open.description: The panel is showing. A press on the trigger toggles it; Esc and a press outside close it.

side.description: Which side of the trigger the panel hangs on. Where that side has no room and the other has more, it flips.

align.description: Which edge of the trigger the panel lines up with along that side (start is the reading start: the left in a left-to-right page). end suits a trigger at the window's right edge, such as an avatar.

width.description: The panel's width; 0 lets it take its content's width.

matchTrigger.description: The panel is exactly as wide as its trigger: a picker under a field.

label.description: The panel's accessible name, when its content does not name itself (a Menu names itself).

bare.description: No card: no fill, edge, corner, shadow or padding. For content that is already a card, such as a Menu.

modal.description: Tab stays inside the panel, and the rest of the page is inert until it closes. Most popovers are not modal.

showTrigger.description: With no children: draws a button the panel belongs to, with the panel in flow beside it, as the catalogue shows it.

children.description: The control the panel belongs to. A press on it toggles the panel; it is told it opens a panel (aria-haspopup), whether it is open (aria-expanded) and which (aria-controls).

notes: The trigger gets aria-haspopup ("menu" with `bare`, else "dialog"), aria-expanded and, while open, aria-controls.
Name the panel with `label` unless its content names itself.
Focus moves into the panel when it opens and back to the trigger when it closes, unless the person moved it elsewhere.

examples.name: Filters
examples.description: A short form hanging under its button.

examples.name: A menu (bare)
examples.description: A Menu is already a card, so the popover draws none round it. end lines it up with a trigger at the window's right edge.

edgeCases.title: Near the edge of the window
edgeCases.handling: When the chosen side has no room for the panel and the other side has more, the panel flips there. Along the side it is kept inside the window with a gap at the edge, and a panel taller than the room scrolls inside itself.

edgeCases.title: Opened from a dialog
edgeCases.handling: The popover is above the dialog in the layer stack: Esc and a press outside close the popover first, and the dialog keeps its own.

edgeCases.title: The page scrolls while it is open
edgeCases.handling: The panel follows its trigger, re-placed on every scroll of any box and on resize. It does not close on scroll.

edgeCases.title: Nothing in the panel can take focus
edgeCases.handling: Focus goes to the panel itself (it is focusable), so Esc still closes it.

web.base: A <div> round the trigger (`children`); while open, the panel (role="dialog", or the content's own role when `bare`) is drawn in the overlay layer: a fixed, full-window box rendered into the nearest AntFabricRoot, so the theme's variables apply and no overflow clips it. Placed from the trigger's box, flipped and kept inside the window, re-placed on scroll and resize; focus moves in and back through useOverlayFocus; `open` through useControllable(open, onOpenChange)
notes: Only the top overlay takes Esc and a press outside: a popover opened from a dialog closes before the dialog does.
On the server, and in the catalogue's pictures, the panel is drawn in place under its trigger; in the browser it moves into the layer before the first paint.
The trigger toggles the panel itself: an app passes `open` and `onOpenChange`, and does not toggle it again from the trigger's own onPress.

keyboard.action: Opens the panel; focus moves to its first control
Closes it; focus goes back to the trigger
Moves through the panel; with `modal` it stays inside

desktop.base: The same panel as web at desktop density

mobile.base: A Pressable round the trigger; while open, the panel is drawn in a transparent Modal over the screen, placed from the trigger's measureInWindow and flipped where there is no room. A press on the backdrop and Android's back close it
notes: `modal` marks the panel accessibilityViewIsModal, so a screen reader stays inside it.

progress-bar.name: Progress bar
progress-bar.description: A thin brand-coloured fill for work with a known size — a file upload, a project's completion — or an indeterminate segment when the size is not known yet. With a title it becomes an upload row: the file, how much has moved, and Cancel.

value.description: 0–100, clamped. The desktop kit calls it pct; the mobile kit takes 0–1 and the adapter multiplies by 100, so one prop means one thing everywhere.

indeterminate.description: The size is not known yet (preparing an export, waiting for the server to accept a file). No value is announced.

label.description: Accessible name of the bar. Left out, the bar says its built-in "Progress" (strings.progress-bar.label); the catalogue's sample names an upload.

tone.description: brand while it moves; success when done; danger when it stopped and needs you; neutral for a quiet measure (storage used).

title.description: Turns the bar into an upload row: the file or job name, one line.

detail.description: How much has moved, in units a person reads: "2.1 of 5.3 MB", "Waiting for a connection", "Upload failed".

action.description: The row's one control: Cancel while it moves, Retry once it has failed.

a11y.label: {label}, else the title, else "Progress"
notes: The bar's name is `label`; without one it is the row's `title` (aria-labelledby on the web), so a list of uploads reads as a list of files, and the default "Progress" only names a bar with no title. `detail` is the value's text (aria-valuetext, accessibilityValue.text): "2.1 of 5.3 MB".

aria-valuenow follows the value. The bar does not announce itself while it moves: a screen reader reads the value when the bar is reached, and an app that wants "done" or "failed" spoken says it itself. Nobody wants "41 percent, 42 percent…".
Indeterminate exposes no value and is aria-busy. The Cancel button's name includes the file: "Cancel upload of Q4 roadmap.pdf".
The web fill moves by transform, not width, and the phone's Reduce Motion setting is followed live.

edgeCases.title: Value out of range or missing
edgeCases.handling: Clamped to 0–100, so 130 draws full and −5 draws empty. A NaN or unknown total becomes indeterminate rather than a bar stuck at zero.

edgeCases.title: Fast enough not to show
edgeCases.handling: An upload that finishes in under 300 ms never draws a bar — the attachment just appears. Once a bar is shown it stays at least 400 ms, then turns to Uploaded.

edgeCases.title: Stalled
edgeCases.handling: No bytes for 8 s: the bar holds where it is (it never fakes motion) and the detail changes to "Waiting for the network…". Cancel stays available.

edgeCases.title: Offline mid-upload
edgeCases.handling: Desktop pauses and resumes from the last acknowledged byte when the connection returns (resumable upload); the message waits in the outbox. The phone refuses new sends while offline, keeps an in-flight upload queued with "Waiting for a connection", and resumes on reconnect — neither counts as a failure.

edgeCases.title: Cancel
edgeCases.handling: Immediate, no confirm — the file is still on the person's device. The partial upload is discarded server-side, the attachment chip leaves the composer, and focus returns to the composer. A second press does nothing.

edgeCases.title: Window hidden in the tray
edgeCases.handling: The upload continues. Progress shows on the Dock icon (macOS) or the taskbar button (Windows; Linux where the desktop supports it). An OS notification is raised only if the upload fails, since that message did not send.

edgeCases.title: Tab in the background, or closed
edgeCases.handling: A background tab keeps uploading. Closing or reloading while an upload runs triggers the browser's leave-page prompt; if the person leaves anyway, the draft is restored with the file marked "Not uploaded" next time.

edgeCases.title: App backgrounded or killed
edgeCases.handling: Backgrounded: a background upload session carries on and the message sends when it completes. Killed: the next launch shows the message with "Upload interrupted" and Retry — the file is still referenced from the device.

edgeCases.title: Reduced motion
edgeCases.handling: Value changes jump instead of easing, and the indeterminate segment stands still in the middle of the track; the detail text ("Preparing…") carries the meaning.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left
edgeCases.handling: The fill grows from the right edge; the Cancel button sits at the left end of the row.

web.base: A role="progressbar" <div> track (aria-valuenow, aria-busy) whose fill eases its width over duration.slow, or slides with the af-indeterminate keyframes; the upload row's Cancel / Retry is the kit's IconButton; inline styles over `t`
notes: While an upload is in flight, closing or reloading the tab asks first (beforeunload); the tab title gains nothing — the composer row is where progress lives.
The indeterminate segment slides with a 1.4 s CSS animation and stops under prefers-reduced-motion.

desktop.base: The same as web: the fill moves by width, as the catalogue drew it
notes: The fill moves by translateX on a full-width bar, not by width and not by scaleX: width re-lays out every frame, and scaleX squashes the pill cap (at 10% the end would be visibly flatter than at 90%). The catalogue draws it with width.
Uploads keep running when the window is hidden in the tray; the Dock icon (macOS) and the taskbar button (Windows) show the total with Tauri's setProgressBar, and clear it when done.
StepBar is a different component (wizard steps: done, current, future).

mobile.base: A View (accessibilityRole progressbar, accessibilityValue) with an Animated fill: the width eases on Animated.timing, the indeterminate segment loops on Animated.loop and parks mid-track under Reduce Motion; the kit's IconButton for Cancel / Retry
notes: 6pt track on surface.muted. Today's API is value 0–1; the kit keeps accepting that and maps it.
Uploads run in a background URLSession (iOS) / WorkManager job (Android) so locking the phone does not stop them.

gestures.action: Stops the upload at once — no confirm; a light haptic

A recording uploads, and Retry picks it up again

progress-ring.name: ProgressRing
progress-ring.description: A value against its goal as a ring, with a label in the middle. It is a share, not a state: it has no thresholds and no colour change of its own. Use a Meter where the value running out or running low matters.

value.description: What is done, in the same unit as `max`. A value past `max` is a full ring.

max.description: The goal: 1 when the value is already a share (0.583 is 58.3%).

size.description: Px (points on the phone). Default 56 on the web and desktop, 48 on the phone (`kpi.ringSize`); the catalogue draws 56 on both.

thickness.description: The stroke's width. 0 is 12% of the size, and never less than 5.

tone.description: default is the first series colour; positive, negative and warning are the data palette's gain, loss and caution.

center.description: The text in the middle, in the chart font. Empty is the share, "58%"; pass what the ring measures ("455") when that is clearer.

animate.description: Draws in once when it mounts, unless the person reduces motion. Off by default.

label.description: The ring's name for a screen reader. Empty says the text in the middle if there is one and the share ("58.3% of the goal"); say what the goal is where the label beside it does not ("Tickets resolved by Fabric, 455 of 600").

a11y.label: The `label` prop, or the text in the middle and the share ("455, 76% of the goal"); the spoken value is the share
notes: The ring is a progressbar with a value: min 0, max the `max`, now the value held to that range, and the share as its text. The middle text is part of it (a progressbar's children are presentational), so it is read once, in the default name.
The chart's pieces are not focus stops: the ring is not in the Tab order at all.
A value that is not a number reads "Progress unavailable" and draws an empty track with an en dash.

examples.name: Q4 goal
examples.description: The middle says what is counted, not the share.

props.label: Approvals cleared within a day, 128 of 150
Docs questions answered, 31% of the target

edgeCases.title: Not started
edgeCases.handling: Zero draws the whole track and no value slice: no round-ended stub at 12 o'clock. The middle says 0%.

edgeCases.title: Past the goal
edgeCases.handling: A value past the max is a full ring, clamped. The middle says 100%: if the real number matters, pass it as `center` ("112%").

edgeCases.title: No goal
edgeCases.handling: A max of zero, or a value or max that is not a number, draws the empty track and an en dash. It never draws a full ring.

edgeCases.title: A small ring
edgeCases.handling: The middle text is one line at caption size whatever the ring's size, so a short share fits a ring of about 40px or more. Below that, or with a longer text, it overflows the hole: keep `center` to the share or a few digits, and put anything longer beside the ring.

web.base: recharts' PieChart at an explicit size: a whole-ring Pie in the track colour under the value's Pie, whose ends are rounded (cornerRadius); the middle is a <span> in the chart font
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is a dependency of the React kit and is reached only from there.

desktop.base: The same recharts PieChart as web, at desktop density

mobile.base: react-native-gifted-charts' PieChart as a donut with two slices (the value, then the track), starting at 12 o'clock and running clockwise, with a Text over its hole
notes: gifted-charts' slices have no round ends, so the phone's ring ends square where the web's is round.
The hole is the card's colour: a ring on a tinted surface shows its edge.

question-panel.name: Question panel
question-panel.description: The one panel every question an agent asks is answered in, docked above the composer: may it run this tool, may it do this, which one, or what should the value be. Nothing is preselected, there is no close, and the agent stays paused until the person answers.

title.description: "Approve this action?" for a tool call or a consent, "Choose one", "Type your answer".

agentName.description: The agent's display name, for the waiting bar and the paused line ("Fabric is paused until you answer."). Empty names none: "Waiting for your approval", "Paused until you answer."

waitingLabel.description: The collapsed bar's words. Empty reads the strings' own: "Waiting for your approval", or "Fabric is waiting for your approval" with an agentName. "Fabric is waiting for your answer" for a choice or a typed answer.

regionLabel.description: The region's accessible name: "Question for you", or the strings' "Approval needed" when empty. It stays when the panel is collapsed.

toolName.description: The tool's own name, printed as it is in a mono chip. Only a gated tool call has one; empty hides the chip.

details.description: What the agent says it will do (a consent's intent). Plain text, never Markdown: it can carry words a model read in someone's email.

args.description: The tool call's arguments as name and value, printed whole as plain text. A long list scrolls; values are never cut.

sample.name: subject
sample.value: Release train: the cut moves to 4pm

sample.name: body
sample.value: Hi both, staging is green. I'll cut the release branch at 4pm and post the checklist in #release-train.

options.description: The answer rows, each with a key, a label and an optional detail line. List refusal first. Nothing is chosen until the person chooses.

sample.label: Approve
sample.detail: Send this email to 2 people now.

field.description: A typed answer instead of rows (ask_user's input kind). Enter submits.

placeholder.description: The typed answer's example. Empty reads the strings' "Your answer".

confirmText.description: Type-to-confirm: choosing the guarded row opens a field, and Submit waits until this is typed exactly (the tool's full name). Empty turns it off.

confirmOption.description: The key of the row type-to-confirm guards. Refusing is never guarded. Empty guards none.

value.description: The chosen row's key. Empty: nothing chosen, so Enter or a stray press answers nothing.

typed.description: What has been typed: the answer in the field, or the confirm text.

expanded.description: The question is shown. False shrinks it to a bar with waitingLabel (the root, folded). The question is still open: answering is the only way out.

autoFocus.description: Moves focus to the question (its title; the phone's screen reader focus) when it appears or expands: for a question that blocks the turn. Either way the question is announced.

offline.description: Submit waits and the footer says why. Rows and typing still work.

sending.description: The answer is on its way: Submit reads Sending… and everything locks, so a second press cannot send a second answer. Pressing Submit sets it; the app removes the panel.

onSubmit.description: The chosen row's key, or the typed answer trimmed. A gated tool reads approve or deny; a choice sends the option's key; a consent sends the sentence the app maps it to.

notes: A region named by regionLabel, in both states. A question that appears or opens is announced (assertive); `autoFocus` also moves focus to the title. The collapse and expand button reports aria-expanded (web).

The rows are a radiogroup labelled by the title. Arrow keys (turned round in right-to-left) and Tab reach every row, rows past nine included. The detail is the row's description (web) or its value, read after the name (phone).
The number keys 1 to 9 choose a row only while focus is inside the panel and never while typing in a field; they are hidden from screen readers.
Long details and the argument list scroll, and take a tab stop with a name ("Details", "Tool arguments") and a focus ring, so a keyboard can read them (web).
Offline, the footer becomes a status and says why Submit waits. On the phone the collapsed bar is one button that names the question and expands it.

examples.name: Type to confirm
examples.description: Approve is chosen, so its confirm field is open.

props.details: Archive #release-train-old and its 214 messages. Members keep read access.

props.title: Choose one
props.waitingLabel: Fabric is waiting for your answer

edgeCases.handling: A hint says so under the field once anything is typed, and Submit stays off. The match is exact and case-sensitive, after trimming what was typed; the text is the tool's full name, server prefix and all.

edgeCases.title: Ten or more answers

edgeCases.title: A long argument
edgeCases.handling: Values are printed whole and wrap; the list scrolls past its height (240 on web and desktop, 220pt on the phone) rather than cutting a value someone is approving.

edgeCases.title: No answers to choose from
edgeCases.handling: A choice with no options can never arm Submit. The app must not ask one; the panel does not invent rows.

edgeCases.title: A number key while typing
edgeCases.handling: Ignored in any input, textarea or editable element, so a 2 typed into the composer stays a 2. Also ignored inside an open dialog and with a modifier held.

edgeCases.title: The connection drops with a row chosen
edgeCases.handling: The choice stays and Submit waits; the footer says the person is offline and can answer once AntFabric reconnects.

edgeCases.title: Answered somewhere else
edgeCases.handling: The app removes the panel when the question closes, wherever it was answered. The panel never resets itself after sending.

radar-chart.name: RadarChart
radar-chart.description: Several scores on shared axes, one polygon per series: how one thing does on six measures, and how it did last quarter. The grid is the scale (the outer ring is `max`), each polygon is a flat fill and a line in its series colour, the legend turns series off, and the tooltip lists every series on the axis it is on. For a few categories and one measure, a BarChart reads more exactly; "View as table" has the numbers.

headingLevel.description: The heading level of the card's title, 1 to 6, so the chart keeps the page's heading order: a card under an h2 is an h3, one under an h1 is an h2. The phone has one kind of header and reads it for nothing. The card is not a landmark: the figure inside is named by the summary.

data.description: Rows, one per axis: [{ area: "Accuracy", q4: 86, q3: 78 }, …]. The same rows can feed a table and a bar chart. Three axes or more make a shape; two make a line.

x.description: The field of each row that names its axis.

y.description: The field, or fields, that are the scores: "q4" or ["q4", "q3"]. One to five, one polygon each; a sixth and after are not drawn. A value that is not a number is 0.

title.description: The card's title. It names the figure on the page, and is the first words of what a screen reader hears.

subtitle.description: One line under the title: what it covers. Empty draws none.
subtitle.sample: Reviewer scores out of 100, by quarter

headline.description: A number to lead with, under the title: { value, format, delta, deltaFormat, inverse, period }. It is a MetricValue (in the chart's format unless it names one), a Delta badge and what the change is against ("resolved in October"). Left out, the card has none.

max.description: What a score at the outer ring is. A score past it is drawn on the ring and a score under zero at the centre; the tooltip and the table still say the real number.

format.description: A format name, its options or a function: what core's `fmt` takes. The axis, the labels at the ends of bars, the tooltip, the summary and "View as table" all print through it, so they agree.

labels.description: A field's name for people, for the legend, the tooltip and the table's headers: { opened: "Opened" }. A field with no entry prints its own name.

height.description: The plot's height, in px (points on the phone). The card is as wide as the space it is given.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when there are no rows. Say why: nothing yet and nothing matching a filter are different sentences.

emptyLine.description: One sentence under it: what to do about it.

loading.description: Grey bars of uneven heights in place of the plot, from the kit's Skeleton, and no "View as table". The header stays, so the card does not jump when the data arrives. Screen readers hear "Loading chart" once.

hidden.description: The series the legend has turned off, by field: ["resolved"]. Left out, the chart keeps its own, starting with every series on. Controlled when the app passes it with `onHiddenChange`.

onHiddenChange.description: A legend entry was pressed. Called with every series that is off now. The last series showing cannot be turned off, so pressing it calls nothing.

a11y.label: The summary: "Fabric's answer quality: Q4 2026: highest Speed (94), lowest Follow-up (68); Q3 2026: highest Speed (90), lowest Follow-up (63)."
notes: The figure is named by the sentence core's `summarize` writes from the rows, categories read as highest and lowest; it is heard, not printed: in the light theme most series colours sit under 3:1 against the card, so the tooltip and "View as table" give the scores without colour.
"View as table" is the other way in, and the better one for exact numbers: one row per axis, one column per series, with real headers.
The legend says what it toggles: each entry is a button that is pressed while the series is on, struck through when it is off. The last series showing cannot be turned off.
A radar is not read polygon by polygon: the summary and the table carry the scores, and the tooltip is never the only place a value is.

edgeCases.title: No rows
edgeCases.handling: An empty `data` draws the kit's EmptyState in the plot's place and says why (the title and line are props); the card keeps its header and has no "View as table" and no legend, since there is nothing to show or toggle.

edgeCases.title: A score over the scale
edgeCases.handling: A score past `max` is drawn on the outer ring, not out past it where it would run into the axes' names; the tooltip and the table still say the real number (112). A score under zero is drawn at the centre.

edgeCases.title: All zero
edgeCases.handling: A series that scored nothing everywhere is a polygon of no area at the centre: the grid is there, the legend still names it and the summary says its highest and lowest are 0.

edgeCases.title: More than five series
edgeCases.handling: A radar draws the first five, on both kits: more are a tangle that no legend untangles. The legend and the table hold the same five. A sixth is a different chart: a table, or a BarChart.

edgeCases.title: A long axis name
edgeCases.handling: Axis names sit outside the outer ring in the room the plot keeps for them, and a long one is the app's to shorten: the tooltip and the table carry the full row.

edgeCases.title: Loading
edgeCases.handling: Grey bars of uneven heights fill the plot and the card keeps its header. There is no legend, no table button and no summary yet. A screen reader hears "Loading chart" once.

web.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a <section>: the title, an optional headline, "View as table" (Button); a ChartFrame holding recharts' RadarChart (PolarGrid, PolarAngleAxis, a hidden PolarRadiusAxis, a Radar per series); the Legend (toggle buttons) in the header beside the Button, as the reference dashboard has it
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: recharts is reached only from there. The chart is handed an explicit width and height.

The grid's rings and spokes, the axes' names in the chart's quiet text, the tooltip and the series colours are the same chart tokens every chart reads (`rechartsTheme()`), and no colour of the brand is.
A polygon is its colour at one opacity (`FLAT_FILL`) and a line, never a gradient. Where two polygons overlap the fills add, which is how you can see Q3 sits inside Q4.
The polygons draw in once over 600ms on the kit's ease-out and tween to new values (a series turned off, new rows); the tooltip glides between axes. Reduced motion turns it off.

keyboard.action: Moves into the plot, then on to the legend's entries and "View as table"
On a legend entry: turns the series off or back on

desktop.base: The same Card, recharts' RadarChart and Legend as web, at desktop density
notes: The same `rechartsTheme()` as web. Hover is the pointer's, so the tooltip follows it; there is no press-and-hold.

keyboard.action: Moves into the plot, then on to the legend's entries and "View as table"
On a legend entry: turns the series off or back on

mobile.base: The kit's Card (pad none) around a View: the same header and Button, a ChartFrame holding react-native-gifted-charts' RadarChart with `dataSet` and a `polygonConfigArray`; the Legend's toggles above the plot
notes: Shipped from the data subpath: gifted-charts and react-native-svg are reached only from there.

gifted-charts' radar applies one opacity to a polygon's fill and line alike, so each series is two polygons in `dataSet`: its fill at `FLAT_FILL`, then its line over it. Its grid and polygon gradients default on and share ids across charts, which draws the wrong colours, so `showGradient` is off on every one and the fills are the tokens'.

gifted-charts' radar has no pointer of its own: the kit finds the axis under a finger from where it lands (core's `nearestAxis`) and draws the tooltip card, so a finger can read each axis as the web's pointer does.
The polygons draw in unless the person reduces motion. Under react-native-web (the catalogue, `pnpm check`) gifted-charts' animation is off, because the values it animates with reach the DOM as text.

radio-group.name: Radio group
radio-group.description: Choose exactly one of a few, all visible at once. The chosen option is marked with a brand-coloured dot — a dot, not a tick, because a tick is the multi-select vocabulary. On the desktop a short answer row can be drawn as pills, where the chosen pill goes ink so it never competes with the primary button. A choice that needs a picture or a few more words (a layout, a plan) is drawn as cards, the chosen one edged in the strong ink.

options.description: [{ key, label, description?, disabled?, preview?, tags? }]. Two to six options; more than that is a Select. `preview` (a node: a small picture of what the option looks like) and `tags` ([{ label, tone? }], the kit's Tag chips after the label: "In use", "Default") are drawn by `appearance="cards"` only.

value.description: The chosen option's key. Empty is allowed and lights nothing — an unanswered question is genuinely unanswered.

label.description: The group's name: the question being answered.

hideLabel.description: Keep the name for screen readers but do not draw it, when a heading above already asks the question.

appearance.description: list is a ring and a label per row. pills is the desktop's ChoicePills — a wrapping row of short answers (Yes · No · Maybe); the phone draws them as the list. cards is a card per option, for a choice that needs a picture or a few more words (a layout, a plan): its `preview` on top, its label with its `tags`, its description. The chosen card takes a 2px edge in the strong ink, not the brand, and draws no ring. Web and desktop lay the cards out in as many columns of at least `radioGroup.cardMinW` (220) as fit; the phone stacks them one per row.

disabled.description: The whole group, for a write in flight or a person who may read but not change it. Say why near it.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: Each option is role=radio with aria-checked; the visible legend is aria-hidden because it is already the group's name. Inside a FormField with no label of its own, the field's label names the group.

The group is one tab stop (the chosen option, or the first when nothing is chosen). The arrow keys move to the next enabled option and choose it, wrapping; with nothing chosen the first arrow press moves too. Left and right follow the direction of the tree.
An option's description is its aria-describedby (the phone: its accessibilityHint). Inside a FormField the group takes the field's description, error, aria-invalid and aria-required.

As cards, the card itself is the radio (aria-checked), so the choice is announced as it is for the list; the card draws no ring, since its edge shows the choice, and its preview is hidden from screen readers. Its name is its label then its tags ("Sidebar In use"; the phone says the tags in its hint, before the description). A card that cannot be chosen is disabled, dimmed and skipped by the arrows.
