switch.name: Switch
switch.description: An on/off setting that takes effect the moment it flips — no Save. On is the tenant's brand colour, never green: both states are fine, and a switch reports a choice, not an outcome. On the phone it is the platform's own switch, shaped like iOS on iPhone and like Material on Android.

description.description: What on means, or why it cannot be turned on right now.

icon.description: A leading glyph saying what the setting is about. The switch says whether it is on.

hideLabel.description: Draw the switch alone, when the row it sits in shows the label. The label stays the accessible name.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: role=switch with aria-checked; announced "Notification sound, switch, on". The track is hidden: the state is in aria-checked.
The description is the control's aria-describedby (the phone: its accessibilityHint); inside a FormField the field's description and error follow it.
The thumb travels toward the end edge, so it moves the other way in a right-to-left tree. The on state is brand-coloured against a grey off track, and keyboard focus draws a ring on the track.

props.label: Push notifications
props.description: Mentions, DMs and replies in threads you follow.

props.label: Private channel
props.description: A channel filed under a project stays private.

edgeCases.title: The OS has notifications turned off
edgeCases.handling: Turning a notification switch on asks for permission the first time. If permission is denied the switch returns to off and the description names the fix, per OS: iPhone "Turn them on in Settings → AntFabric → Notifications." Android "Allow notifications for AntFabric in Settings → Apps." macOS "Allow AntFabric in System Settings → Notifications." Windows "Turn on notifications for AntFabric in Settings → System → Notifications." Browser "Your browser is blocking notifications for this site." Each with an Open Settings action where the OS allows deep-linking.

edgeCases.title: A server-backed change fails
edgeCases.handling: The thumb moves at once. If the write is refused it moves back and a toast says "Couldn't change Push notifications. Try again." Toggling again while a write is in flight is allowed; writes coalesce and the last value wins. Offline on the phone, account settings refuse with "You're offline. Try again when you're connected." and the switch does not move.

edgeCases.title: Changed on another device
edgeCases.handling: Account settings sync: turning mentions off on the phone moves the desktop's switch in place. Device settings (Notification sound, Show Notifications on desktop, Bluetooth proximity on the phone) never sync — each describes this machine.

edgeCases.title: Switch or checkbox
edgeCases.handling: A switch applies immediately. Anything confirmed by a Save button, or a choice in a list of several, is a checkbox. Inside a menu it is always a checkbox row (menuitemcheckbox) — the desktop ⚙ menu's two settings are exactly that.

edgeCases.title: A muted rail must not look normal
edgeCases.handling: With Show Notifications off and the window hidden in the tray, nothing tells the person they muted it — so the rail's ⚙ stays visibly loud while either switch is off, and the tray menu shows "Notifications paused".

edgeCases.title: Reduced motion
edgeCases.handling: The thumb jumps instead of sliding and the track colour changes without a fade. iOS's own switch honours the system setting itself.

edgeCases.title: Text scaled to 130%
edgeCases.handling: The label and description wrap; the switch stays the platform size and is centred on the row. The whole row stays the tap target.

web.base: <button role="switch"> with aria-checked, inline styles over `t`; the thumb slides by a CSS transform transition; hover and focus from useInteraction; `checked` through useControllable
notes: Use a switch only where the change applies immediately. In a form with a Save button, the same setting is a checkbox.

Browser notifications: turning "Show Notifications" on is the moment to call Notification.requestPermission() — from the click, never on page load. If the browser says denied, the switch returns to off and the description says "Your browser is blocking notifications for this site."

Pressing toggles `checked` (an `on.press` action, so the catalogue preview is interactive): the thumb slides by transform (track width − padding − thumb) over 180ms and the track colour fades with it.

keyboard.action: Toggles
Toggles (it is a button)

desktop.base: The same <button role="switch"> as web: a 30×18 track with a 14px thumb that slides 12px
notes: Desktop has no switch today. The notification rail's ⚙ menu holds its two settings, Notification sound and Show Notifications, as menuitemcheckbox rows with the square check, and that stays: ARIA has no menu-item switch, and inside a menu the tick IS the control.
This switch is for settings screens and rows outside menus (Preferences → Notifications), where the same two settings appear with the same labels.
While either notification setting is off, the rail's ⚙ button stays loud (surface.muted under text.body) so a mute is never invisible.
Notification sound and Show Notifications are device settings (lib/notify-prefs.ts) — they do not sync to the phone.
Pressing toggles `checked`: the thumb slides 12px by transform while the track fades to the brand colour.

keyboard.action: Toggles

mobile.base: Pressable (accessibilityRole switch) drawing each OS's own shape — UISwitch's 51×31 on iOS, Material's 36×14 track under a 20dp thumb on Android — not RN's Switch, so the catalogue and the app match; the thumb slides with Animated.timing; `checked` through useControllable
notes: On track is colors.primary — the tenant's primary — never a literal, so a white-labelled build keeps its own brand.
Off track is switchTrackOff and the thumb is switchThumb (white in both themes), the nearest roles to UISwitch's own; surfaceSunken vanished on a dark card.
iOS draws a 51×31 UISwitch. Android's RN Switch is Material: the colours apply, the iOS shape does not — the catalogue draws each OS's own shape.
Used as the trailing control of a settings row (Push notifications, Bluetooth proximity); the row's label is the switch's accessibilityLabel.
Tapping toggles `checked`: the thumb slides by transform, 20pt on iOS and 16dp on Android, as the native switches animate it.

gestures.action: Toggles with a light haptic (iOS draws its own)
Toggles on release (iOS)

tab-bar.name: Tab bar
tab-bar.description: The phone's navigation: a floating 56pt pill of four tabs and, beside it, the Fabric disc that opens the assistant. The chosen tab is a 100pt tinted capsule with its icon over its label; the others are icons alone. Scrolling a list squeezes the bar down to a 42pt circle holding the current tab, and it steps aside while the keyboard is up.

tabs.description: NavItem: { key, label, icon, badge?, max?, badgeLabel? } left to right. Meetings never badges — a schedule is not a backlog.

active.description: The key of the open tab. A key no tab has ("none" while a pushed screen is on top) draws no capsule: the tabs share the width evenly.

expanded.description: The tabs are shown. Left (false) is the bar squeezed by scrolling down: a 42pt circle with the current tab's icon. Scrolling up or a tap opens it again.

keyboardUp.description: The bar is not drawn while the keyboard is up.

safeArea.description: Draws a picture of the home indicator (iOS) or gesture handle (Android) beneath, to show the bar sits 12pt above the safe area. A real app has the system's own: leave it off.

action.description: ActionItem: { key, label, icon?, badge?, disabled? }. The floating round button beside the bar; its `label` is its accessible name. Leave it out for none.

notes: Each tab is role tab with selected state, so VoiceOver says 'Messages, tab, 1 of 4, selected'. Badges join the name: 'Inbox, 12 new'.
Squeezed, the hidden tabs and the disc leave the accessibility tree and the circle is one button: 'Show tabs. Messages is open'.
Reduce Motion is followed live: turning it on in Settings stops the capsule's growth and the lens's spring on the next change, with no restart.
Dynamic Type: the bar and each tab take a minimum height, so they grow with the text; labels are capped at 1.3x, and from a 1.3x font scale every tab shows its label, not only the open one.
A bar holds five tabs: each keeps at least the 44pt touch width, and a sixth makes the bar wider than the screen. A development build warns; put the rest behind a "More" tab.

edgeCases.title: Badge counts
edgeCases.handling: Each tab caps at 9+; the number is the same server count as the desktop rail and the home-screen icon badge. Recording counts untranscribed recordings, Meetings never badges.

edgeCases.title: The keyboard is up
edgeCases.handling: The bar steps aside entirely (it owns no input, so nothing is lost) and the screen's reserve drops to the keyboard's own inset. It returns when the keyboard hides, without animating over the composer.

edgeCases.title: Long labels and 130% text
edgeCases.handling: The capsule stays 100pt; its label is capped at 1.3× and truncates with an ellipsis ('Besprechu…'). The full label is the tab's accessible name. The other tabs are icons, so scaling never crowds them.

edgeCases.title: Small phones
edgeCases.handling: At 320pt wide the three idle tabs get (track − 100) / 3 each, about 44pt — still the minimum hit area. Nothing below 320 is supported.

edgeCases.title: Reduced motion
edgeCases.handling: No springs: the capsule jumps to the new tab, the squeeze snaps, and the icon motions (bell ring, mic pulse) do not play.

edgeCases.title: Android three-button navigation
edgeCases.handling: The bottom inset is the 48dp button bar instead of the gesture handle; the bar still sits 12pt above it, and the system bar's background follows the theme so the buttons stay legible.

edgeCases.title: App killed, reopened from a notification
edgeCases.handling: A cold start from a push lands on the right tab with the message pushed on top; the bar appears with that tab selected and badges from the push payload until the socket refreshes them.

edgeCases.title: Liquid Glass and earlier iOS
edgeCases.handling: On iOS 26+ the floating pill and its squeezed circle are Liquid Glass, so the content scrolling under them shows through. The glass follows the iPhone's own settings with no work from us, because the kit draws it with the system material (GlassView): Clear or Tinted (Settings → Display & Brightness → Liquid Glass) changes how much shows through, Reduce Transparency makes it frosted and nearly opaque while keeping its shape, and Increase Contrast adds a contrasting edge. The app subscribes to AccessibilityInfo 'reduceTransparencyChanged' only to adjust what it draws around the glass. iOS before 26 keeps the blur look. This happens live in the app as the person changes the setting.

edgeCases.title: The selection lens on iOS 26
edgeCases.handling: On iOS 26+ the selection becomes a glass lens while the finger is down and follows it across the tabs. Releasing outside the bar cancels and the lens returns to the current tab. Reduce Motion keeps the lens but removes the stretch and the overshoot. VoiceOver users switch tabs by swiping, so no gesture is needed. On iOS 18 and Android the bar has no lens: a tap moves the tinted capsule.

web.alternative: nav-rail. Web and desktop navigate with the left rail — 64px of icons, 248px with labels. A phone-sized browser is offered the mobile app rather than a web bottom bar.

desktop.alternative: nav-rail. The desktop's one persistent navigation column; the assistant is the rail's first row rather than a floating disc.

mobile.base: Views and Pressables (accessibilityRole tablist / tab, accessibilityState.selected) in StyleSheet over useTheme() tokens, with Badge and Icon. The pill and the squeezed circle are GlassSurface, so iOS 26+ draws them as Liquid Glass. Each tab's capsule and width (flex-grow 1 → 1.7) move on React Native Animated; on iOS 26+ the selection lens is a PanResponder over the tabs driving an Animated GlassSurface (clear): springy lift, follows the finger, settles on release. In the app it is the tabBar of expo-router's <Tabs>, under react-native-safe-area-context's bottom inset
notes: Drawn over the screens (absolute), 12pt above the safe area on the 12pt gutter; a scrolling tab keeps bottomBarReserve free at its foot so the last row is never under the bar.

Nothing is laid out by React: positions come from two springs on the UI thread, so on a switch the capsule stretches toward the new tab and its back edge catches up ('liquid', owner 2026-10-15). The catalogue draws the resting state.
The capsule is the bar's tint (#FDE8E8, --brand-tint) with a coral icon and label (ADR-9406). The label is 12, the app's type floor, not the component set's 10.
Fabric is a pushed screen on the root stack (ADR-9414): it covers the bar, so the bar has no list of routes to hide on.
Today: only Messages is built (the other three are blank), and no tab has a badge. Per-tab badges are new in this spec, capped at 9+.
Light haptic on every tab press and on the Fabric disc.

iOS 26+: Liquid Glass — the surface is drawn through expo-glass-effect's GlassView (gated on its availability check; the material itself follows the device's Clear / Tinted, Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast settings). iOS 18 and earlier keep today's blur/opaque look. The selected capsule keeps its tint on top of the glass; the Fabric disc stays brand-tinted, as a prominent control does on iOS 26.

Pressing a tab sets `active`: the capsule grows toward it (flex-grow spring) while the old one shrinks, and the label fades in. Pressing the squeezed circle expands the bar again. The bar keeps both itself until the app passes them back (useControllable), reporting through onActiveChange and onExpandedChange, so the catalogue preview is interactive.

iOS 26+: the selection lens. Touching the bar lifts the selected capsule into a larger clear-glass lens (about 1.2×). Dragging moves it across the tabs, stretching with speed and magnifying the icon beneath. Releasing settles it into that tab with a spring and selects it. A tap does the same in one motion. In the kit: a PanResponder claims a sideways drag from the tabs and drives an Animated GlassSurface on the JS driver (its width and position are layout); a tap stays the tab's own press, so VoiceOver and Switch Control activate tabs as usual. The haptic on each tab crossed is the app's, since the kit has no expo-haptics. iOS 18 and Android keep the tinted capsule that flows to the pressed tab.

table.name: Table
table.description: Rows and the columns that say how to read them. Web and desktop draw a grid in a scroll region with a sticky header, right-aligned figures and a sort button on each column; the phone draws one card per row. Sorting, ticking rows and paging are the table's own, and each reports its change.

columns.description: One per column: { key, label, cell, align, format, priority, sortable, rank, tones, inverse, kind, width, maxWidth, wrap, emphasis }. `width` and `maxWidth` (px) and `wrap` are for web and desktop: a cell wider than `maxWidth` is cut with an ellipsis and its full text is the cell's title, or wraps with `wrap`. `emphasis` (web and desktop) draws the column that names the row stronger: `fg.strong` at medium weight, the `emphasis` part; on the phone the row's name is its card's title. `key` is the field of each row the column reads and `cell` is what it draws: text, number, currency, percent, date, delta, badge, tag, avatar, sparkline or progress. A column is plain data, so it can be written down and sent as JSON.

rows.description: One object per row: [{ key: "acc-1", account: "Northwind Logistics", arr: 186000, … }, …]. The same rows can feed a chart, a stat and a table.

rowKey.description: The field of each row that names it, for selection and for React's keys. The keys `selected` holds are its values as text. A row without the field is named by its index in `rows`.

sort.description: { column, direction } with direction "asc" or "desc": the column the rows are ordered by and which way. `null` is the order the rows came in. Left out, the table keeps its own order.

onSortChange.description: A header was pressed (the phone: the sort Select or its direction button). The first press on a column sorts it, biggest first for a number or a date and A to Z for the rest; the second reverses it; the third gives back `null`, the order the rows came in.

selectable.description: A box before each row to tick it, and one in the header that ticks every row on the page (a dash when only some are ticked). The phone puts the same box on each card and one above the cards.

selected.description: The keys of the ticked rows (each row's `rowKey` field, as text). Rows on other pages stay ticked.

onSelectedChange.description: A box was pressed. Called with every key that is ticked now, on this page and the others.

pageSize.description: Rows a page. Over that many rows, a Pagination sits under the table. 0 shows every row.

total.description: How many rows there are in all, when `rows` holds only the page on show (a list the server pages and sorts: an ERP list of 40,000 records). The table then draws exactly the rows it is given, never sorts or slices them, and only reports `onSortChange` and `onPageChange`; the pager counts pages from `total` and `pageSize`. Left out, `rows` is every row and the table sorts and pages them itself. Past about 200 rows, set `pageSize` or page on the server: the table draws every row of a page and does not window them.

currency.description: An ISO 4217 code for the currency columns that name none in their `format`. Numbers, dates and the sort's alphabet follow the tree's locale.

maxHeight.description: The most px the table is tall: past it the rows scroll under the sticky header. Left out, the table is as tall as its rows and the header has nothing to stick to.

renderCell.description: Draws a cell yourself: it is called with the column and the row and RETURNS what goes in the cell (a link, a button). Returning `undefined` keeps the column's own cell. On the phone it draws that value on the card.

renderActions.description: Draws a row's actions (a menu, a button) and RETURNS them: in a last column with a hidden "Actions" header on the web, at the end of the card's head on the phone.

onRowPress.description: A row was pressed. On the web its first cell is a button (so the row is reachable by keyboard) and a click elsewhere on the row does the same, except on a box or a button inside it; on the phone the card's title is a button and a tap on the card does the same.

expanded.description: The keys of the cards that show every column. A card with columns it does not show (a column with no `priority`, or one past the card's three lines) has a button that opens them as more label and value lines.

onExpandedChange.description: A card's details button was pressed. Called with every key that is expanded now.

page.description: The page on show, counted from 1. Sorting goes back to page 1.

onPageChange.description: A page button, previous or next was pressed, or a new sort sent the table back to page 1. Called with the page, counted from 1.

loading.description: Grey lines in place of the rows (the phone: grey cards), from the kit's Skeleton. The header stays, so the columns do not jump when the rows arrive.

empty.description: The title of the empty state when there are no rows. A noun phrase, not a sentence: "No accounts match".

emptyLine.description: One sentence under the title: what to do about it ("Clear a filter to see more."). Empty draws only the title.

dense.description: Shorter rows (36px against 44px), for a table that is mostly data. The phone's cards have one size.

narrow.description: What the table does when its own box is narrower than `table.cardsBelow` (600px), measured with a ResizeObserver on the table, not the window: `scroll` keeps the grid and scrolls it sideways; `cards` draws the phone's card per row (the `priority` columns: the title, a badge beside it and the row's actions, then a label and value line for every other column) with a sort bar above and the pager under them. Ticking, sorting, paging, `onRowPress`, `renderCell`, `renderActions`, loading and the empty state all work in both. Before it has measured (on the server) a `cards` table draws cards.

label.description: What the table is: its caption and the scroll region's accessible name (the phone: the list's). One or two words.

a11y.role: table, in a labelled region (web, desktop); a list of cards (phone)
a11y.label: The `label` prop: the table's caption and the scroll region's name
notes: Each sortable header carries aria-sort (ascending, descending or none) and holds a button with a visible focus ring. A press says "Sorted by ARR, descending" (or "Sorting cleared") through a polite announcement, since a reader on the button does not speak the header's aria-sort. Sorting moves no focus.
Rows arriving after loading ("12 rows loaded") and the rows running out ("No rows") are announced once.

A row's box is named for the row ("Select Northwind Logistics"), the header's "Select all on this page", and it reads mixed while only some rows are ticked. The ticked state is the box's: the row itself carries no aria-selected, which a plain table does not support.
With `onRowPress` the first cell is a button, so the row is a keyboard stop; with `renderActions` a last, visually hidden "Actions" header names that column.
Loading is marked aria-busy and announced once, "Loading Accounts"; the other grey lines are hidden from screen readers.
A sparkline and a meter in a row are named for the row and the column ("Northwind Logistics, 6 months: 140, 148, …"), and a Delta says which way it moved and whether that is good.
Phone: each label and value line of a card is one stop ("Seats used: 86%"), and the box and the details button stay their own. A card's title is a button when `onRowPress` is given.
Colour is never the only signal: a badge is a word, a Delta has an arrow, a ticked row has a ticked box.

examples.name: Accounts
examples.description: Every cell type, sorted by ARR, five rows a page.

examples.name: Health, by rank
examples.description: A text column that sorts by a rank, not the alphabet: at risk first.

examples.name: Rows ticked
examples.description: Two accounts ticked: their rows are filled, and the header's box shows a dash.

examples.name: Name emphasised
examples.description: The column that names the row has `emphasis`: its cells are drawn in the strong ink at medium weight, the rest in body text. A theme that sets `table.headRadius` also rounds the header row's ends.

examples.name: Cards when narrow
examples.description: `narrow="cards"` in a box narrower than `table.cardsBelow`: a card per row, the account its title and health its badge, then a line per other column, under the sort bar. Two accounts are ticked.

examples.name: Cards loading
examples.description: A `cards` table while its rows load: grey cards under the sort bar.

examples.name: Dense
examples.description: 36px rows, for a table that is mostly figures.

props.label: Accounts
props.emptyLine: Clear a filter to see more.

edgeCases.title: No rows
edgeCases.handling: An empty `rows` draws the kit's EmptyState (a title and, if there is one, a line) where the rows go, under the header. Say why: nothing yet and nothing matching a filter are different sentences.

edgeCases.title: A missing value
edgeCases.handling: A value that is not there (null, an empty string, NaN) draws an en dash in every cell type, never an empty Tag or an Avatar with no face. In a sort it goes last, whichever way the column is sorted.

edgeCases.title: More rows than a page
edgeCases.handling: Past `pageSize` rows the table pages, and ticked rows stay ticked on the pages you leave: the header's box ticks the rows on the page you are looking at. Sorting orders every row, then goes back to page 1.

edgeCases.title: A long name
edgeCases.handling: A cell keeps one line. On the web a column grows with its widest cell and the table scrolls sideways when it must; on the phone the card's title and values are cut with an ellipsis.

edgeCases.title: A narrow box with nothing to show
edgeCases.handling: A `cards` table with no rows draws the same EmptyState as the grid, under the sort bar, and says why. With no sortable column and no `selectable`, there is no sort bar at all.

edgeCases.title: Columns with no priority
edgeCases.handling: The phone's card keeps the columns that have a `priority`, lowest first; the rest stay in the grid on web and desktop (and, with `narrow="cards"`, as lines after the card's own). A table whose columns have no priority at all shows the first four, in order.

web.base: A native <table> in a scroll region (tabindex 0), drawn from its recipe: sticky <th>, a sort <button> in each sortable header, the kit's Checkbox, Tag, Avatar, Delta, Sparkline and Meter in the cells, Skeleton rows and EmptyState; hover from useInteraction
notes: Shipped from the data subpath. Core's `@antfabric/ui-core/chart` holds what both kits agree on: how a column is read, how rows are ordered and paged, what the phone's card keeps.

The header sticks to the top of the scroll region. A table that is as tall as its rows never scrolls the region, so it has nothing to stick to: pass `maxHeight` (or give the table a parent with a height) and the rows scroll under the header.
A column is as wide as its widest cell. Wider than the region, the table scrolls sideways; the region is a keyboard stop, so the arrow keys scroll it.

`narrow="cards"`: below `table.cardsBelow` (600px) of its own width the table draws the phone's card per row instead of the grid, a description list of label and value lines per card, under a sort bar (the kit's Select and an IconButton). It measures its box before paint, so a page drawn in the browser never shows the other layout first; drawn on the server it starts as cards and turns into the grid once it measures a wide box. The web's card shows every column (the card's own lines, then the rest): it has no details button.

keyboard.action: Moves to the scroll region, then through the sort buttons and the boxes
On a sort button: sorts by that column, then reverses it, then clears it
On a box: ticks or unticks the row, or every row on the page
In the focused scroll region: scrolls the rows

desktop.base: The same <table> as web, at desktop density

keyboard.action: Moves to the scroll region, then through the sort buttons and the boxes
On a sort button: sorts by that column, then reverses it, then clears it
On a box: ticks or unticks the row, or every row on the page

mobile.base: A View per row, as a card (decision D3): the title column beside its box and a badge, then label and value lines. A sort bar above holds the kit's Select and an IconButton; Pagination below is compact
notes: One card per row. The column with the lowest `priority` is the card's title, a `badge` column among the next three sits beside it, and the rest are label and value lines. A column with no priority is left off the card; when none has one, the columns' order is the priority.

Sorting is the sort bar above the cards: the Select picks a column (the same first direction as the header's first press) and the arrow button beside it reverses the direction. "As listed" clears the sort.
A card's height is its content, and `table.rowH` (52pt) is the least a one-line card is.
`dense` and `maxHeight` have no meaning here and are not props on the phone.
The card shows the title and three more columns, lowest `priority` first; the other columns are not dropped: the card's details button opens them in place as more label and value lines (`expanded`).

Opens the sheet of sortable columns

tabs.name: Tabs
tabs.description: A row of labels on a hairline rule with one brand-coloured bar under the chosen one. It switches what part of a view you are looking at: the channel shelf (Messages, Pinned, Files, Canvas), Upcoming and Past inside a project's Meetings, a phone screen's top filter. A tab may carry a count of how many are in it. On desktop the single bar slides between tabs.

items.description: [{ key, label, badge?, badgeMore?, title?, disabled? }]. disabled draws the tab dimmed and skipped by the arrows and by a press. badge is how many are in there, never how many need you, so it is a quiet bordered chip and never the brand colour; 0 or missing draws no chip. badgeMore draws 100+ for a count from a capped read. title is a tooltip for a one-word label whose scope is not in the word.

value.description: The chosen tab's key. A value that matches no item is allowed and draws no bar, for a strip whose panel can be closed. Never default to the first item.

full.description: Tabs share the SPARE width of the strip (flex 1 0 auto), labels centred, and the bar spans its tab's share. For a narrow column such as the project rail; a wide pane keeps its labels left.

rule.description: Draws the hairline the bar sits on. false only when the container already draws that divider, so there is one line with one owner.

label.description: The strip's accessible name.

panels.description: The product draws a tabpanel for each tab with the id <id>-panel-<key>: each tab then names it in aria-controls. <id> is the strip's id, or a generated one.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: Each tab is role=tab with aria-selected / accessibilityState.selected; aria-selected is also what the sliding bar measures, so there is one way of saying chosen.

On the web each tab has the id `<id>-tab-<key>` (the strip's `id`, or a generated one); with `panels` it also names `<id>-panel-<key>` in aria-controls, for the tabpanel the product draws. The kit draws no tabpanel itself.

Arrow keys follow the page direction (in rtl, ArrowRight goes to the previous tab) and skip a disabled tab; a disabled tab is aria-disabled / accessibilityState.disabled, dimmed, and not selectable by press.
The chosen tab is scrolled into view when it changes (web: scrollIntoView, phone: scrolled to the middle of the strip).
Known gap: on the web the strip clips its focus ring (the strip scrolls, and a scroll box clips an outset shadow); the neutral theme draws the ring inset instead.
The count chip is hidden and joins the tab's name: "Files, 12", or "Assets, more than 100" for a capped count.
A tab whose label does not say its scope carries a title ("Files shared in this channel"), which the tooltip host shows.

edgeCases.title: Nothing chosen
edgeCases.handling: A value that matches no tab draws no bar at all. The channel shelf depends on it: with the details or thread panel open, no shelf tab is showing, and a bar under Files would be the strip telling a lie. When a tab is chosen again the bar is placed there, not slid in from where it last was. Tab then lands on the first tab.

edgeCases.title: More tabs than room
edgeCases.handling: Labels never wrap and never truncate: a two-line tab changes the strip's height and moves everything under it. The strip scrolls sideways instead, with no visible scrollbar and a 16px fade at whichever edge has more. Choosing or focusing a tab scrolls it fully into view. On web and desktop a vertical mouse wheel over the strip scrolls it sideways, because most mice have no horizontal wheel.

edgeCases.title: A huge count
edgeCases.handling: The chip caps at 99+ so one tab cannot outgrow its neighbours; the exact number stays in the tab's accessible name. A count from a capped read (one page of 100) is drawn 100+ with badgeMore, at least this many, never a bare 100 that reads as a fact (ADR-1026), and is announced as "Assets, more than 100".

edgeCases.title: A count that arrives after the strip draws
edgeCases.handling: No chip until the count is known, never 0 and never a skeleton. When it arrives the tab widens, and the bar re-measures in the same frame: each tab is observed, not just the strip, because a tab can grow inside a strip that does not (ADR-9991, the Assets 334 bug). That re-measure only places the bar; a resize is never a journey.

edgeCases.title: No swipe between panels on the phone
edgeCases.handling: Swiping the content left or right does not change tab. Horizontal swipes already belong to the rows (Notifications: swipe left for Mark read and Clear, ADR-9418) and to iOS's back gesture from the edge; a panel swipe would fight both. Tabs change by tapping the strip.

edgeCases.title: Text scaled to 130%
edgeCases.handling: Tabs grow taller with the text (font scale is capped at 1.3×) and the bar stays on the rule. A strip that fitted at 100% and no longer does at 393pt becomes scrollable rather than wrapping or shrinking a label.

edgeCases.title: Reduced motion and right-to-left
edgeCases.handling: With reduced motion the desktop and web bar jumps to the chosen tab instead of stretching across; the label inks still cross-fade, since a colour change is not motion. The design tokens' global reduced-motion rule handles this, so the component adds no check of its own. In Arabic or Hebrew the tabs run right to left, ArrowRight moves toward the end of the reading order, and the bar travels leftward to the next tab.

edgeCases.title: Keyboard only and screen readers
edgeCases.handling: Only the chosen tab is in the tab order; the arrows move and select (automatic activation, because every panel here is already loaded or shows its own skeleton). The focus ring is drawn around the label. VoiceOver and TalkBack read "Mentions, 3, tab, 3 of 3"; selecting announces through the selected state only, with no live region.

web.base: A <div role="tablist"> of <button role="tab"> with a roving tabindex, inline styles over `t`; ← → Home End select; the brand bar under each tab scales in with a transform transition; `value` through useControllable(value, onValueChange)
notes: Web uses the desktop's values (a 32px strip, 12px labels). The web profile's taller controls do not apply here: a tab strip is not a row of buttons.

When the tabs switch a routed view (a project's Meetings, a person's profile), each tab is a link (Tabs.Tab render={<Link>}), so the URL holds the choice, Back returns to the previous tab, ⌘-click opens it in a new browser tab and a shared link lands on the same tab.
The bar animates left and right separately, the leading edge in 180 ms and the trailing edge in 250 ms, so it stretches toward the new tab and its tail catches up, as on desktop.

keyboard.action: Moves to and selects the previous / next tab; wraps at the ends
Selects the first / last tab
Leaves the strip for the panel; only the chosen tab is in the tab order

desktop.base: The same tablist as web at desktop density
notes: The bar is ONE absolutely positioned element that travels (ADR-0518). It is 2px tall and sits 1px below the strip so it covers the hairline: it reads as a break in the rule, not a second line. The catalogue draws a bar under every tab, scaled to nothing except under the chosen one, so pressing a tab (it sets `value`) shrinks the old bar while the new one grows: the nearest a static renderer gets to the travel.

The motion moves the travel edges separately, not with a transform: the edge in front arrives in 180 ms and the one behind in 250 ms, ease-out. The cross axis is placed, never eased, so a strip being resized never animates.

Underlined tabs have no horizontal padding, so the bar is exactly as wide as the word. Labels are semibold whether chosen or not, so nothing changes width while the bar is moving; only the ink changes (text.strong chosen, text.faint not, ADR-1097).

Two uses are sanctioned: a strip inside a pane a segmented strip already chose (Upcoming / Past, ADR-0664), and the channel shelf (ADR-1093). A segmented strip never goes inside a segmented strip; the inner one is always this.
Pass rule={false} when the container draws the divider: the channel shelf puts a + beside its tabs, so the band owns the one line (ADR-1096).
New in this spec: horizontal overflow (today the strip squeezes its labels), arrow-key roving focus (today the tabs are plain buttons), and a label-ink hover for unchosen tabs.

keyboard.action: Moves to and selects the previous / next tab
Selects the first / last tab

mobile.base: A horizontal ScrollView (accessibilityRole tablist) of Pressable tabs (accessibilityState.selected), StyleSheet over useTheme(); the bar scales in with Animated.timing; `value` through useControllable(value, onValueChange)
notes: Top tabs sit directly under a pushed screen's header: edge to edge, with the rule across the full width and the first label on the 12pt gutter.
44pt tall, 14pt semibold labels, 16pt apart. The bar is under the word; each tab gets 8pt of hitSlop either side so neighbouring targets meet with no dead space.
The bar does not slide on the phone. It moves to the chosen tab on the render after the tap, as V2's filter chips do ("No smooth motion").

The chosen label is ink, not the brand colour. ReactionsSheet's hand-built strip draws its chosen label in the brand colour today; this spec keeps the brand colour for the bar only, as on desktop, and that sheet moves onto this component.
Choosing a tab that is partly off screen scrolls it fully into view, as FilterChips does.
Pressing a tab in the catalogue sets `value`; the bar there shrinks and grows between tabs, which the kit does not do (it just moves on the next render).

New on the phone: the Notifications screen's All / DMs / Mentions and the channel details tabs do not exist yet. Today the channel's Pinned and Files are a ⋮ menu (ADR-8921) and the Messages list filters with chips.

gestures.action: Selects the tab, with a selection haptic; an unchosen label darkens while pressed
Scrolls the strip when the tabs do not fit

tag.name: Tag
tag.description: A small square-cornered label for metadata — a status, a priority, a kind. The corner is the meaning: pills are actions and counts, a 5px tag is a fact about the row it sits in, so it never reads as clickable.

tone.description: One colour family per tone in every theme: grey, BLUE, green, amber, red, purple. brand is blue, not coral — coral is the brand fill and means it needs you; a status tag is neither.

icon.description: Optional leading glyph, 12px. Use it when the word alone is ambiguous at a glance (lock for Private), not as decoration.

size.description: md is the platform's own tag: 2 × 8 on web and desktop, 4 × 8 on mobile so it sits in a 44pt row. sm is 2 × 8 everywhere, for the phone's densest rows.

notes: The label is the meaning; colour only repeats it. Never ship a tag whose tone is the only thing that says "blocked".
No role and no live region: a tag is read as part of its row's text. A tag that changes (In review → Approved) is announced by whatever changed it, not by the tag.

edgeCases.title: Label longer than the row allows
edgeCases.handling: One line, truncated with an ellipsis at whatever width the row gives it. The full label is the tooltip on web and desktop and the accessible text everywhere. Write tags as one or two words; a sentence belongs in the row's subtitle.

edgeCases.title: Colour is not the message
edgeCases.handling: Red and green tags differ to a colour-blind reader only by their words, so the words must differ: Blocked and Shipped, never two tags that both say Status. Under forced-colors the fill is gone and a 1px outline in the system colour keeps the shape.

edgeCases.title: Dark mode
edgeCases.handling: Each tone has its own bg/fg pair per theme (the color.tag.* roles), tuned to at least 4.5:1 on both. The status tokens are not reused — inverting only the fill is what made the old dark tags unreadable.

edgeCases.title: Someone tries to click it
edgeCases.handling: Nothing happens and nothing hovers: no cursor change, no fill change. If the surface needs "click a status to filter by it", that surface renders a Chip. A square tag that sometimes responds teaches people to click every tag.

edgeCases.title: Many tags on one dense row
edgeCases.handling: A 30px desktop row never wraps. Show the two most specific tags and a neutral "+3" tag whose tooltip lists the rest; the full set is in the item's detail view.

edgeCases.title: Text scaled to 130%
edgeCases.handling: The tag grows with the type (padding stays 4 × 8). In a ListItem the tags wrap under the title rather than squeezing the title to one truncated word.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left
edgeCases.handling: The icon leads on the right. Directional glyphs mirror; the lock and the sparkle do not.

web.base: A <span> (no role, not focusable) with the full label as its title tooltip, on the color.tag.* roles; a transparent outline becomes its shape under forced colours; inline styles over `t`
notes: Not a button and not focusable. A tag that filters a list is a Chip (a pill that takes a press), never a pressable Tag.
Under forced-colors (Windows High Contrast) the fill disappears, so the tag keeps its shape with a 1px outline that the browser draws in the system colour (the kit sets it transparent).

desktop.base: The same <span> as web, at desktop density
notes: Reads the tag's OWN colour roles (--tag-*, ADR-5325), not the status roles. Borrowing --success-soft drew Light's dark ink on a dark slab in the dark themes, at 1.9–2.8:1.
Semibold, not bold (owner, 2026-09-26) — the weight My Tasks and Rituals were already overriding every tag to.
One size today (2 × 8). The full label is the tooltip when the row truncates it.
No press and no entrance: a tag is read, not used. When a status moves on (In review → Shipped) the fill and ink cross-fade over 150ms instead of snapping.

mobile.base: View + Text (numberOfLines 1, maxFontSizeMultiplier 1.3) on the color.tag.* roles; StyleSheet over useTheme()
notes: Today's mobile component is called Badge and is this label. It is renamed Tag so that Badge means an unread count on every platform, as it does on the desktop.

The mobile Badge's `primary` (coral) and `accent` tones fold into brand (blue) and info (purple), following the desktop Tag (owner, 2026-10-01: "update the components based on the desktop components").
A status DOT keeps the status inks (StatusDot) — it is a signal, not a tag, and is not this component.
Font scale is capped at 1.3× (maxFontSizeMultiplier), as everywhere in the app.

text-area.name: Text area
text-area.description: Several lines of text with its label, a help line, an error and an optional character count: TextField's multi-line sibling, with the same anatomy and states. Hover moves the fill, focus draws a 2px grey edge, invalid paints the edge red and wins over focus. `mono` sets the text in the monospace face for code, JSON and templates.

label.description: Visible label and the field's accessible name. Always pass one: with `hideLabel` it is still the name a screen reader says.

value.description: The text. Left out, the field keeps its own text, starting from `defaultValue`, and still reports each change through onValueChange.

defaultValue.description: The text a field with no `value` starts with: a form that only reads the field when it is sent.

placeholder.description: An example of the answer, never the instructions — placeholders vanish the moment someone types.
placeholder.sample: What this channel is for, and who should join it

rows.description: How many lines tall the field is. On the web the person can drag it taller (`resize`); on the phone it is the least it is tall and it grows with the text.

mono.description: Sets the text in the monospace face (`font.mono`) at the regular weight, for code, JSON and templates. Spellcheck, capitals and autocorrect are off and the text is laid out left to right.

name.description: The name a form posts this field under.

resize.description: vertical draws the browser's grip in the field's corner, so the person can drag it taller; none keeps it at `rows`. The phone's field grows with its text instead.

helper.description: One clause under the field. Replaced by the error while invalid.
helper.sample: Shown under the channel name in search and in the channel list.

error.description: What is wrong and how to fix it, shown in place of helper while invalid is true.

required.description: Sets aria-required and draws a "Required" tag beside the label, as TextField does.

maxLength.description: Caps typing at this many characters and shows the count. 0 is no cap and no counter.

disabled.description: Skipped by Tab and not announced as editable. Say why in helper.

readOnly.description: The text can be read, selected and copied but not changed. Stays in the tab order — use this, not disabled, for anything someone may need to read.

hideLabel.description: Hides the label and the tag visually, for a field whose heading already says what it is. The label stays the field's accessible name.

onBlur.description: Focus left the field: the moment to check the value and set invalid.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: The label is a real <label for> (the phone: the accessibility label); with `hideLabel` it is hidden visually and still the name.

The helper or the error and the counter are the textarea's aria-describedby (the phone: its accessibility hint) and the field sets aria-invalid; an error that appears is announced once, politely. Required is aria-required (the phone: said after the name).
The counter is not a live region. When typing pauses within the last 10% of the limit (at least 5 characters) the characters left are announced, and reaching the limit is announced once.

examples.name: Monospace template
examples.description: `mono` for JSON and templates: the monospace face, no spellcheck, laid out left to right.

props.helper: Placeholders in double braces are filled in when the webhook fires.

examples.name: Label hidden
examples.description: The label is the accessible name only: the heading above the field already says what it is.

edgeCases.title: Longer than its rows
edgeCases.handling: On the web the text scrolls inside the field past `rows` lines and the person can drag the grip to make it taller; on the phone the field grows with the text. Long lines wrap; nothing is cut.

edgeCases.title: At the character limit
edgeCases.handling: maxLength stops the keystroke rather than explaining a truncation afterwards; a paste that overruns is cut at the limit and the field announces "Character limit reached" once.

edgeCases.title: Required and invalid
edgeCases.handling: The "Required" tag sits beside the label; an error replaces the helper and is announced once. Format errors appear on blur, never on the first keystroke.

web.base: <label for> + <textarea data-af-input rows> in a drawn box, inline styles over `t`; hover and focus from useInteraction on the box (the 2px edge is a 1px border plus a 1px inset ring, so nothing shifts); the error, the helper and the counter are tied to the textarea by aria-describedby; `value` through useControllable
notes: The textarea fills its box and carries the inset, so the resize grip sits in the box's corner. `resize="none"` removes the grip.
Inside a FormField the field supplies the id, aria-describedby, aria-invalid and aria-required, as it does for TextField.
Enter types a new line: a text area never submits its form on Enter.

keyboard.action: Moves into the field; disabled fields are skipped, read-only ones are not
Starts a new line

desktop.base: The same <label> + <textarea> as web, at desktop density

keyboard.action: Moves into the field
Starts a new line

mobile.base: A multiline TextInput (textAlignVertical top, font from the recipe, placeholderTextColor, maxFontSizeMultiplier fontScale.content) in a View box from the recipe; its least height is `rows` lines of the input's line height plus its inset; an error and the characters left are announced with announceForAccessibility; `value` through useControllable
notes: The field grows with its text from `rows` lines; there is no resize grip on a phone, so `resize` and `name` are web props.
`mono` uses the system's monospace face (Menlo on iOS, monospace on Android) and turns off capitals and autocorrect.

gestures.action: Focuses and raises the keyboard
The system's select / copy / paste menu — available on read-only fields too

text-field.name: Text field
text-field.description: One line of text with its label, a help line, an error and an optional character count. Each state owns one dimension: hover moves the fill, focus draws a 2px grey edge, and invalid paints the edge red — and invalid wins over focus, because a field you are typing into that is still wrong must keep saying so.

label.description: Visible label and the field's accessible name. A field with no visible label still needs one for screen readers — pass it and the kit hides it visually.

placeholder.description: An example of the answer, never the instructions — placeholders vanish the moment someone types.

type.description: What the field holds. It sets the input type on the web and, on the phone, the keyboard, capitals and autocorrect, and secure entry for password. An address, a number or a password is laid out left to right.

name.description: The name a form posts this field under, and a password manager files it by.

autoComplete.description: What the browser or the phone may fill in: email, username, current-password, new-password, one-time-code, tel, off.

inputMode.description: The keyboard a phone browsing the web app raises, when type does not already say: a code of digits is numeric.

prefix.description: Fixed text before the value that is not part of it, like the # of a channel name.

leadingIcon.description: Field furniture in text.faint, one step smaller than the text. Never tinted on focus — the edge already says which field is active.

trailing.description: A control at the end of the field: Copy on a read-only link. A password's Show is `reveal`.

reveal.description: With type password: a Show / Hide button at the end of the field. On, the characters are shown until it is pressed again; its accessible name says Show password or Hide password, and aria-pressed says which.

helper.description: One clause under the field. Replaced by the error while invalid.
helper.sample: Lower case, no spaces. We will tidy it for you.

error.description: What is wrong and how to fix it, shown in place of helper while invalid is true.

tag.description: A one-word pill beside the label — "Beta", "Optional".

required.description: Sets aria-required and, with no tag, draws a "Required" tag.

maxLength.description: Caps typing at this many characters and shows the count. 0 is no cap and no counter.

size.description: lg is the 44px dialog and wizard field. sm is the 32px toolbar field. The phone has one 48pt field.

disabled.description: Skipped by Tab and not announced as editable. Say why in helper.

readOnly.description: The value can be read, selected and copied but not changed. Stays in the tab order — use this, not disabled, for anything someone may need to read.

focused.description: Draws the focus edge without real focus — for the catalogue, screenshots and a form's jump-to-first-error. At runtime the kits track focus themselves.

copied.description: A trailing Copy was just pressed: the field announces "Copied" politely and clears it after 1.5s. The Copy control passed in trailing swaps its own glyph to a check and its name to "Copied" from the same state, held by the caller.

onSubmit.description: Enter (the phone: the keyboard's Return key) was pressed in the field. Not fired while an IME is composing.

onBlur.description: Focus left the field: the moment to check the value and set invalid.

a11y.label: {label}
notes: The label is a real <label for> (the phone: the accessibility label, falling back to the placeholder); the placeholder is never the name unless there is no label.

The helper or the error is the input's aria-describedby (the phone: its accessibility hint) and the field sets aria-invalid; an error that appears is announced once, politely. Required is aria-required (the phone: said after the name).

The counter is part of the description, read when the field is focused; it is not a live region. When typing pauses within the last 10% of the limit (at least 5 characters) the characters left are announced, and reaching the limit is announced once.
`type` sets the input type and, on the phone, the keyboard and secure entry; an address, a number or a password is always laid out left to right.
Inside a FormField the control takes the field's id, description, error, aria-invalid and aria-required.

examples.name: Password with Show
examples.description: type password and reveal: the characters stay hidden until Show is pressed.

examples.name: Invalid while focused
examples.description: Invalid wins over focus: the edge stays red and thickens to 2px.

edgeCases.title: The phone gets an error state
edgeCases.handling: Mobile's Input had no invalid look; forms printed a red line under it. Now the edge turns danger (2pt while focused), the message sits under the field with an icon, replaces the helper, and is announced once. A light warning haptic plays only when a submit is refused, never while typing.

edgeCases.title: A long value or a long error
edgeCases.handling: The value stays on one line and scrolls inside the field; it never wraps or grows the field. The label truncates with an ellipsis. The error wraps to as many lines as it needs — an error is never truncated, because the cut-off half is usually the instruction.

edgeCases.title: At the character limit
edgeCases.handling: maxLength stops the keystroke rather than explaining a truncation afterwards. A paste that overruns is cut at the limit and the field announces "Character limit reached" once. The cap on the control matches the server's, so nothing is clamped silently on save.

edgeCases.title: Read-only, not disabled
edgeCases.handling: Anything someone may need to read or copy is read-only: it stays in the tab order, is announced "read only", and can be selected and copied. Disabled is skipped by Tab and a screen reader may not read it at all. Either way the helper says why it cannot be changed — a greyed box that cannot account for itself is a dead end.

edgeCases.title: Validation timing
edgeCases.handling: Format errors appear on blur, never on the first keystroke; once shown, the error clears as soon as the value becomes valid. Server answers (a name already taken) come back after a round-trip and never clear what was typed. A save that fails offline keeps the value and says "You're offline. Your changes are kept here."

edgeCases.title: Text scaled to 130%
edgeCases.handling: 48pt is a minimum: the field grows with the text and the label wraps to two lines rather than truncating. Entry text and labels scale up to 2×.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left and mixed-direction values
edgeCases.handling: The prefix and leading icon sit at the start edge and the counter at the end. The input sets dir="auto", so an Arabic or Hebrew value aligns right inside an English interface and a Latin slug aligns left inside an RTL one.

edgeCases.title: Keyboard covers the field
edgeCases.handling: The form scrolls the focused field (and its error line) above the keyboard. Return reads Next and moves to the following field; the last field's Return reads Done or Send.

edgeCases.title: IME composition
edgeCases.handling: While a Japanese, Chinese or Korean IME is composing, Enter confirms the candidate and does not submit, and validation waits for compositionend — otherwise a half-composed word is judged and the form submits mid-word.

web.base: <label for> + <input type="text" data-af-input> in a drawn box, inline styles over `t`; hover and focus-within from useInteraction on the box (the 2px edge is a 1px border plus a 1px inset ring, so nothing shifts); the error and helper are tied to the input by aria-describedby; `value` through useControllable
notes: The error is announced through aria-describedby on the control plus aria-invalid; Field.Error renders only while invalid, so a screen reader is not told about an error that is not there.

Set type, autoComplete and inputMode for what the field holds (email, url, one-time-code) so browsers autofill it and phones browsing the web app get the right keyboard. Inside a FormField the field supplies the id, aria-describedby, aria-invalid and aria-required.

Focusing the field draws the edge; `focused` draws it without real focus. A read-only field's Copy is the caller's control: it swaps its own glyph and name while the field's `copied` announces "Copied".

keyboard.action: Moves into the field; disabled fields are skipped, read-only ones are not
Submits the surrounding form
Inside a dialog, closes the dialog — the field never swallows it

desktop.base: The same <label> + <input> as web: lg 44px on --radius-input, sm 32px on --radius-control
notes: Hover moves the FILL only (surface.hover) and never on an invalid or focused field; focus is a 2px border.active edge with no halo (ADR-0421). The edge is drawn so it takes no room — the text never shifts 1px when the field takes focus.

The 2px grey edge measures 1.57:1, under WCAG 2.2's 3:1 for a focus indicator. ADR-0421 records that as the cost of the owner's explicit call (width, not a darker grey); it is a known gap, not an oversight.

lg 44px uses --radius-input (11); sm 32px uses --radius-control (9). These are the desktop's --control-h-input and --control-h-sm, which the shared token profile does not carry yet, so they are written as numbers here.
Spellcheck and autocorrect are off for names and slugs (spellcheck=false), on for prose fields.

Pressing the field sets `focused`: the 2px edge fades in over 150ms. Copy on a read-only field sets `copied` (check glyph, "Copied" name) and the kit clears it after 1.5s. An error, when it arrives, fades in under the field.

keyboard.action: Moves into the field
Submits the dialog the field is in

mobile.base: TextInput (fontFamily set by font(), placeholderTextColor, maxFontSizeMultiplier fontScale.content, keyboard and secure entry from `type`) in a View box over a StyleSheet from useTheme(); focus draws a 1pt inset boxShadow ring over the 1pt edge; the error fades in through <Enter motion="fade">; `copied`, an error and the characters left are announced with announceForAccessibility; `value` through useControllable
notes: 48pt minimum, --radius-input 11, a 1pt edge drawn as a Rim over the edge so it takes no room; focus thickens it to 2pt border.active, never the brand colour.

The phone had no error state; this spec adds one: a danger edge (2pt while focused) and the message under the field with an icon, replacing the helper. LabeledInput's error line was colour-only; the icon is added so the error does not rely on colour.
The TextInput sets fontFamily itself — it does not pass through the kit's Text, and without it the field renders in the platform font.

The entry text grows with the person's text size up to 2× (reading text), like the label, and the field's height is a minimum. A secure (password) field remounts when revealed and refocuses, because iOS caches secureTextEntry on the native view.
Tapping the field sets `focused` and the 2pt edge fades in; Copy on a read-only field sets `copied`, with a success haptic.

gestures.action: Focuses and raises the keyboard; the screen scrolls the field above it
The system's select / copy / paste menu — available on read-only fields too

thinking-indicator.name: Thinking indicator
thinking-indicator.description: An agent's turn in flight, where its answer will appear: a coral lattice rippling in the avatar's column, a word that changes every few seconds, how long it has been, and once it runs a tool, the steps folded underneath. It goes the moment the agent writes or asks.

steps.description: Every tool call this turn, oldest first, as AgentSteps draws them. Empty while the agent is only thinking: no caret, no fold.

agentName.description: The agent's display name, for what a screen reader hears ("Fabric is running Draft email"). Empty names none: "Thinking", "Running Draft email".

words.description: The word beside the lattice, rotating through these every few seconds. Empty shows the strings' word ("Thinking") and keeps it still.

since.description: When this stretch began (epoch ms), from the app's state, so leaving the screen and coming back does not restart the clock. 0 counts from when it mounts.

expanded.description: The steps are unfolded. The caret folds them; only drawn once there is a step.

notes: What the agent is doing now ("Fabric is running Draft email via …") is announced through the page's live region as it changes, not the rotating word, which is hidden with the mark and the clock.
Once there are steps, the head is a button named from its word and what it does ("Thinking… Show steps") with aria-expanded.

Reduced motion follows the setting live (on the web after mount, so server and first client render agree; on the phone as it changes): the lattice holds at 60%, the word stops changing and shimmering. The phone's clock ticks in a child of its own, so the indicator does not re-render ten times a second.

edgeCases.title: A long turn
edgeCases.handling: The clock reads seconds to a tenth under a minute, then minutes and seconds (1m 05s). Past five steps (three on the phone) the oldest are counted as "+N earlier".

edgeCases.title: Switching screens mid-turn
edgeCases.handling: Pass since from the app's state: the clock carries on from when the turn began instead of starting again at 0.0s.

edgeCases.title: Fabric writes, then runs a tool
edgeCases.handling: The app hides the indicator at the first word and shows it again under the text when a tool starts. The panel's question turns it off: Fabric is waiting, not working.

web.base: A role=status row drawn from its recipe: the lattice on the kit's af-lattice (648 ms, each ring 135 ms later), the word clipped to an af-shimmer gradient, a clock painted every 100 ms without re-rendering; the fold is a grid-rows transition

desktop.base: The same row, where Fabric's next message will start
notes: Today's desktop gives each lit cell a soft coral glow; this kit leaves it out, as no shadow token says it yet.
It shows while a turn is in flight and nothing is written yet, comes back when Fabric goes to a tool after writing, and goes when Fabric asks a question (assistant-core's showsThinking).

mobile.base: Views on Animated's native driver: each cell's ripple, the word breathing between 45% and full, the clock re-rendered every 100 ms; the steps unfold without an animation
notes: Today's phone sweeps a gradient band across the word through an SVG mask (react-native-svg and Reanimated). This kit breathes the word instead, as it uses neither; the owner may want the sweep.
Today's phone restarts the clock when the screen remounts; since keeps it running.
The phone's word is 14pt against the desktop's 13, its mark column 30pt against 32, and it shows three steps, not five.

Fold the steps away

thread-summary.name: Thread summary
thread-summary.description: The line under a message that has replies: who is in the thread, how many replies, how many you have not read, and when the last one came. Pressing it opens the thread.

replyCount.description: Replies in the thread. 0 renders nothing — the parent message decides whether to draw the summary at all.

lastReply.description: Relative time of the newest reply, formatted by the caller: "just now", "12m ago", "2h ago", "Yesterday", "Monday, 27 October".

participants.description: Up to three repliers, most recent first: { name, identity, src?, agent? }. The caller trims the list; more than three is never drawn.

unreadCount.description: Replies you have not read. Server-counted (it rides the message beside reply_count) because the client holds no replies until the thread is opened.

following.description: You follow this thread: you started it, replied, were mentioned in it, or chose Follow. Followed threads notify you and appear in Threads.

onFollowingChange.description: Called with `following` as the press leaves it. Given `following` too, the line is controlled and the press changes nothing on it; on its own (the catalogue, where opening is navigation) the press flips Following.

onPress.description: Opens the thread: the side panel on web and desktop, the thread screen on mobile.

a11y.label: Open thread, 4 replies, 2 unread, last reply 2h ago
notes: The faces are hidden from assistive tech; the label carries the facts in reading order.
Unread is said in words as well as drawn in blue, never by colour alone.
Counts are grouped in the reader's locale (`useLocale()`): 1,204 or 1.204.

edgeCases.title: Hundreds of replies and an old last reply
edgeCases.handling: The count is written in full with the locale's grouping (1,204 replies) and never truncates. "Last reply …" is the part that gives way: one line, ellipsis, and the full time is in the label.

edgeCases.title: Read on another device
edgeCases.handling: Opening the thread on the phone clears the unread count on the desktop and web through the same read-state event as the sidebar badge. Reading the channel does NOT clear it: the channel's read mark stops at the newest top-level message, so a newer reply stays unread here after the sidebar badge has gone.

edgeCases.title: Root deleted, replies remain
edgeCases.handling: The summary stays under the "This message was deleted." tombstone so the conversation in the thread is still reachable. Pressing it opens the thread with the tombstone as its root.

edgeCases.title: Offline
edgeCases.handling: The desktop draws the summary from its SQLite cache, so counts and faces may be stale; opening the thread shows the cached replies under the offline notice. Nothing pretends the count is live.

edgeCases.title: Offline on web and mobile
edgeCases.handling: The last known count stays drawn; pressing it opens the thread screen, which shows the replies already loaded in this session or "You're offline. Showing what's on this device." when there are none.

edgeCases.title: A reply arrives while you are looking
edgeCases.handling: The count and "Last reply" update in place; the line never moves the message under the reader's eye because its height does not change. Your own reply never counts as unread.

edgeCases.title: Text scaled to 130%
edgeCases.handling: The line may wrap after the count; faces stay on the first line, and the target grows with the text rather than clipping it.

web.base: A <button> with inline styles over `t`; hover, press and focus from useInteraction; faces from the kit's Avatar (xs).
notes: Opens the thread in the right-hand panel and updates the URL (…/c/platform-eng/t/<id>), so a thread is a link that can be pasted, bookmarked and opened in a new tab with ⌘-click.
Hover lifts it to a card edge (Slack's) so it reads as a button and not as the message's text.
Opening the thread is navigation, so in the catalogue a press toggles `following` instead (what Follow / Unfollow in the thread's ⋯ does): the bell and 'Following' fade in or out.

keyboard.action: Opens the thread panel
On a focused message, opens its thread — the same target

desktop.base: The same <button> as web (one file), at the desktop density; faces from the kit's Avatar (xs).
notes: Today's desktop draws the thread glyph, "N unread" in info blue and "N replies" in coral (ADR-4007: two numbers in one colour read as one fact). This spec adds the repliers' faces, "Last reply …" and Following.
The count uses the link ink (coral) and the unread uses info blue, so the two numbers stay apart at a glance.

keyboard.action: Opens the thread panel
On the message cursor, opens its thread

mobile.base: Pressable over a wrapping row, StyleSheet over useTheme() tokens (44pt target), usePress for the pressed fade; faces from the kit's Avatar (xs).
notes: 14pt SemiBold, coral count, info-blue unread — the V2 Figma. The whole line is one 44pt-tall target even though the text is 20pt.
On a 375pt screen "Last reply …" is what gives way first: it truncates, then the faces stay, then Following stays — the count and unread never truncate.

gestures.action: Pushes the thread screen

title-bar.name: Title bar
title-bar.description: The desktop window's top strip, drawn by the app rather than the OS. macOS floats the traffic lights over it; Windows and Linux get a ☰ application menu on the left and their own window controls on the right. In between: visible Back / Forward / History buttons and a search field that opens the command palette.

canGoBack.description: False at the first place visited this session. The history is in memory and starts empty on every launch.

history.description: Draws the Recent history button after Back and Forward.

search.description: Draws the search field in the middle.

searchPlaceholder.description: The field's text. Empty uses the `searchPlaceholder` string ("Search"); a product says what it searches.

searchKeys.description: The palette shortcut, drawn per OS: ⌘K on macOS, Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux.

fullscreen.description: macOS full screen. The system hides the traffic lights, so the 96px inset drops back to 16.

maximized.description: Windows and Linux. The maximise glyph becomes restore.

focused.description: False while another app's window is in front. macOS greys the traffic lights; Windows and Linux dim the caption glyphs.

menuOpen.description: Windows and Linux: the ☰ application menu is open (see app-menu-bar).

sidebarExpanded.description: The nav rail is open (248px with labels). The sidebar button before Back draws panel-left-close then, panel-left-open otherwise, and its name says which way it goes.

actions.description: IconActionItem: { key, label, icon, badge?, disabled? }. Icon buttons before the window controls, after `trailing`; `label` is the accessible name.

trailing.description: Transient status before the actions — the recording indicator while the microphone is live. Empty the rest of the time.

onSidebarExpandedChange.description: The sidebar button was pressed, with the width it leaves the rail: pass it to NavRail as `expanded`.

onSearch.description: The search field was pressed: open the command palette.

onMenuOpenChange.description: Windows and Linux: ☰ was pressed, with `menuOpen` as it leaves it.

onMinimize.description: Windows and Linux caption button. macOS draws its own traffic lights.

onMaximize.description: Windows and Linux: Maximise, or Restore when `maximized`.

onClose.description: Windows and Linux: Close, which hides the window to the tray (ADR-0379).

notes: Back and Forward are real buttons that are natively disabled when there is nowhere to go: they are announced as dimmed and leave the tab order, and the bar's layout does not shift.
The Windows and Linux ☰ is a menu button (aria-haspopup="menu", aria-expanded follows `menuOpen`). The menu itself is the app's (AppMenuBar) and keeps its own keys and focus.

The traffic lights are drawn by macOS and are hidden from the page's accessibility tree; VoiceOver reaches them as the window's own close / minimise / zoom buttons. Windows and Linux caption buttons are not tab stops, as the native ones are not.
The search button says what it opens: 'Search people, channels and projects', with the shortcut in its tooltip.
The search field is centred in the window however wide the controls on either side are; the sides are never narrower than their controls, so in a narrow window the field gives way first.

examples.name: Sidebar open
examples.description: The nav rail is expanded, so the sidebar button offers to collapse it.

edgeCases.title: macOS full screen
edgeCases.handling: The system hides the traffic lights in full screen, so the bar stops reserving 96px and returns to its 16px inset (useWindowFullscreen, read on mount and on every resize). Moving the pointer to the top edge reveals the macOS menu bar over the window; the bar does not move for it.

edgeCases.title: Window in the background
edgeCases.handling: macOS greys the three lights while another app is frontmost; Windows and Linux dim the caption glyphs to 45%. The rest of the bar keeps its colours — dimming the search field would read as disabled.

edgeCases.title: Maximised on Windows
edgeCases.handling: The maximise square becomes the overlapping 'Restore down' squares. Double-clicking empty bar toggles it; dragging a maximised window down by the bar restores it under the pointer (Aero Snap), which data-tauri-drag-region gives for free.

edgeCases.title: Nowhere to go back to
edgeCases.handling: After a launch the history is empty, so Back and Forward are both disabled. ⌘[ is still swallowed (preventDefault) so it can never navigate the webview out of the app. An open dialog suppresses history navigation — going back under a dialog would lose what someone was doing.

edgeCases.title: Drag versus click
edgeCases.handling: Only the bar's empty space drags. A press that starts on a button and moves is a cancelled press, not a window drag. Double-clicking the search field opens the palette once and never maximises the window.

edgeCases.title: Right-to-left system language
edgeCases.handling: macOS moves the traffic lights to the top-right in Arabic and Hebrew, and Windows mirrors the caption buttons to the left. The inset follows the lights to whichever side they are on; Back points right and Forward points left.

edgeCases.title: Narrow window or high zoom
edgeCases.handling: The window's minimum is 1180×720, but View › Zoom In to 175% leaves about 670 CSS pixels. Below 900 CSS px the search field collapses to its magnifier, and below 720 Help moves into the ☰ / app menu. History buttons never collapse — they are the only on-screen way back.

edgeCases.title: Keyboard and screen reader
edgeCases.handling: Tab order: ☰ (Windows/Linux), Back, Forward, History, Search, Help. Window controls are skipped, as the native ones are. F6 moves between the title bar and the regions below it, so nobody has to tab through the rail to reach search.

edgeCases.title: Hidden in the tray, then reopened
edgeCases.handling: Close hides the window (ADR-0379) and leaves full screen first (ADR-0811). Reopening from the tray or the Dock restores the same history, so Back still works after a hide; only Quit empties it.

edgeCases.title: Liquid Glass and earlier macOS
edgeCases.handling: On macOS 26+ the title bar loses its fill and divider and the controls become glass capsules; on 15 and earlier it is today's solid chrome bar. macOS 26's own glass follows the Mac's settings by itself. Our title-bar capsules are drawn in the web view, so the Tauri shell reads NSWorkspace's accessibilityDisplayShouldReduceTransparency and accessibilityDisplayShouldIncreaseContrast, listens for the display-options-changed notification, and passes both to the page, which switches the capsules to the tinted, solid or high-contrast material (glass.tinted, glass.solid, shadow.glassContrast), live, as the setting changes (prefers-contrast is the fallback). Reduce Transparency makes the capsules frosted and nearly opaque; Increase Contrast adds an edge. macOS before 26 keeps today's solid bar.

web.alternative: web-top-bar. In a browser the browser owns the window frame, the tabs and its own Back / Forward; the page draws a 44px top bar inside the viewport instead, with no window controls and no drag region.

desktop.base: A <div role="banner"> whose empty strips carry data-tauri-drag-region, for Tauri 2's window chrome (macOS: titleBarStyle "Overlay", trafficLightPosition {x:16, y:24}; Windows/Linux: decorations false + shadow true). IconButton for ☰, the sidebar button, Back / Forward / History and Help; the search field is a <button> with a Kbd hint; the macOS lights are drawn in place (aria-hidden), Windows' caption buttons and GNOME's round ones are <button tabIndex=-1>. Inline styles over `t`, hover / press / focus from useInteraction, `menuOpen` and `sidebarExpanded` through useControllable; on macOS 26 the bar goes transparent and the sidebar button, history and search become glass() capsules.
notes: Today: macOS overlays the traffic lights on the breadcrumb row with a 96px left inset (TRAFFIC_LIGHT_INSET, ADR-5322) and Windows/Linux keep the native title bar and native menu bar. The ☰ button, the custom Windows/Linux bar and the visible Back / Forward / History buttons are new in this spec — today history is only ⌘[ / ⌘] (ADR-6130) with nothing on screen.
The 96px inset follows trafficLightPosition.x (16) plus three 12px buttons 20px apart. Change tauri.conf.json, tauri.staging.conf.json and this inset together.

Every empty pixel of the bar carries data-tauri-drag-region; every control does not, so a click on a button is never a drag. Double-click on empty bar zooms (macOS, per System Settings › Desktop & Dock › 'Double-click a window's title bar to') or maximises (Windows, Linux).
The search field is a button that opens the command palette (a modal search over people, channels and projects), not an input — the same decision NavRail's SearchControl records.

Windows: decorations false loses the Windows 11 Snap Layouts flyout on the maximise button. Ship it with the tauri-plugin-decorum hit-test (HTMAXBUTTON) or accept the gap; Win+Z still opens Snap Layouts. shadow: true keeps the 1px border, drop shadow and resize edges.

Linux: controls follow GNOME's org.gnome.desktop.wm.preferences button-layout — stock GNOME draws only Close, Ubuntu draws all three, and a layout like 'close,minimize,maximize:' puts them on the left. Tiling compositors (Sway, Hyprland, i3) get no controls at all.
Window controls are not tab stops on Windows, matching the native caption buttons; Alt+Space opens the system window menu instead.
Windows and Linux: pressing ☰ toggles `menuOpen`, so the button holds its pressed look while the application menu (app-menu-bar) is open.

The sidebar button opens and closes the nav rail. It sits after the traffic lights (or ☰) and before Back, outside the rail, where shadcn's sidebar puts its trigger and macOS apps put theirs; the rail holds only navigation. onSidebarExpandedChange hands the app the width for NavRail's `expanded`. Today's desktop draws this button under the rail's lockup (NavRail.tsx); this spec moves it here.
In a narrow window the two sides keep their controls (the lights or ☰, the sidebar button and history; Help and the window controls) and the search field narrows first, down to its minimum.

macOS 26+ (Tahoe): the toolbar has no bar of its own — the history arrows and the search field float as Liquid Glass capsules over the content, as Tahoe's own apps do. Built with Tauri's macOS window effects; if the platform can't draw glass, it falls back to the macOS 15 look. Windows and Linux are unchanged.

keyboard.action: Back, to where you just were (the Back button)
Forward again
Opens the command palette (the search field)
Windows and Linux: opens the ☰ application menu with File highlighted
Windows: the system window menu (Restore, Move, Size, Minimise, Maximise, Close)
macOS: enters or leaves full screen; the traffic lights hide and the inset collapses
Moves focus between the title bar, the rail, the sidebar and the conversation

mobile.alternative: mobile-header. A phone has no window: the status bar and safe area belong to the OS, Back is the header's chevron or the system back gesture, and search is a field on each tab screen.
